items.title: Cloud Storage Bucket Enumeration via Predictable Naming
items.prerequisites: Basic knowledge of the target organization's naming conventions (from OSINT: company name, product names, environment labels like dev/staging/prod). A bucket-enumeration wordlist tool (S3Scanner, GCPBucketBrute, or a custom script) and network access to the relevant cloud provider's storage API endpoints.
items.whatItIs: Cloud storage buckets (like AWS S3 or Azure Blob) are often named in predictable ways based on the company or product name — things like 'companyname-prod-backups' or 'companyname-dev'. That predictability lets an attacker guess likely bucket names and simply check each one to see if it exists and whether it's publicly readable, without knowing anything in advance.
items.rootCause: Buckets get named this way for internal clarity — so engineers can tell at a glance what a bucket is for. But that same clarity makes the name guessable from outside. Combined with the fact that cloud storage lets anyone check whether a given bucket name exists at all, the naming convention itself becomes the main thing standing between an attacker and finding it.
items.impact: If a discovered bucket also has weak access rules, enumeration is the step immediately before full data exposure. Even when the bucket itself is properly locked down, confirming it exists still helps an attacker. They learn the organisation's naming pattern, which gives them a validated target list for guessing other bucket names and a set of internal conventions to reference in a convincing social engineering approach.
stepsToIdentify: Gather OSINT on the organization's naming conventions from job postings, GitHub repositories, public documentation, and its known domain names/product names.

Generate a candidate bucket-name wordlist combining the company/product name with common suffixes (-prod, -dev, -staging, -backup, -uploads, -logs, -assets, -public, -private, -data) and common separators (hyphen, underscore, no separator).

Run an enumeration tool (S3Scanner for AWS, GCPBucketBrute for GCP, or a manual HTTP HEAD-request loop for any provider) against the candidate list to identify which names resolve to an existing bucket.
For each existing bucket found, separately assess its access policy (public listing, public read, public write) since existence alone is only the initial identification step, not proof of exposure.
Establish whether a discovered bucket is genuinely public or merely predictably named, since the name alone is not exposure — the access policy is.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cloud storage enumeration for the target organization's known cloud accounts/domains.
Build and run the candidate-name wordlist against the relevant cloud provider's storage-existence-check endpoint.
For each bucket confirmed to exist, attempt an unauthenticated listing/read request to determine its actual access policy.

Where a bucket is found to be both enumerable and publicly accessible, escalate testing to the specific publicly-accessible-bucket finding for full impact assessment rather than treating enumeration alone as the complete finding.

Document every discovered bucket name (existing, regardless of access level) as evidence of the naming-convention predictability, distinct from the separate access-control findings for any bucket found actually exposed.

examplePayloads.label: Automated S3 bucket enumeration against a wordlist
Manual existence check via HTTP HEAD (AWS S3)
GCP bucket brute-forcing
Azure Blob container enumeration

variants: Enumeration of storage accounts/containers themselves (the parent resource) rather than just individual bucket names, relevant to Azure's storage-account naming model.
Enumeration combined with typo-squatting variants of the legitimate bucket name to catch misconfigured or forgotten copies.
Enumeration seeded from the organisation's own naming pattern observed on one known bucket, which yields sibling buckets across environments far faster than a generic wordlist.
mitigation: Avoid embedding the company or product name directly in bucket names; use a randomized or non-guessable identifier (a UUID-based suffix) instead, especially for any bucket that will hold sensitive data.
Apply the principle of least privilege to every bucket's access policy regardless of naming, since naming obscurity is not a substitute for correct access control.
Enable logging on storage-access APIs and monitor for high-volume existence-check/enumeration patterns against the account.

Where cloud-provider tooling allows it, restrict bucket-existence-check responses (some providers offer options to return a uniform response regardless of existence to reduce enumeration feasibility).
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your cloud storage containers are named in a predictable pattern, which lets an attacker guess their names and probe each one to see if it is readable. Naming is not the vulnerability by itself — a guessed name only matters if the container is also left open — but predictable naming turns a needle-in-a-haystack search into a quick checklist. The durable protection is to ensure no container is publicly readable regardless of its name, using the provider's account-wide setting that blocks public access outright. Treat the naming as a reason not to rely on obscurity, and the access setting as the actual control.

items.title: Insecure Cloud DNS Zone Takeover
items.prerequisites: DNS enumeration tools (dig, dnsx, or a subdomain-takeover-specific scanner like Subjack or can-i-take-over-xyz's fingerprint database). Access to register/claim the specific cloud resource the dangling record points to (e.g. an Azure/AWS/GitHub Pages account) if demonstrating full exploitation, which should only proceed with explicit client authorization given the account-creation step involved.
items.whatItIs: A DNS record (usually a CNAME) points to a cloud resource — a storage bucket, a hosted app, a CDN — that's since been deleted, but the DNS record itself was never removed. Since most cloud providers let anyone claim a resource name that's no longer in use, an attacker can register that exact same name, and the company's own still-live DNS record will now send visitors straight to infrastructure the attacker controls.
items.rootCause: Deleting a cloud resource and deleting the DNS record that pointed to it are two separate steps, and nothing reliably ties them together. When a team removes the resource but forgets the DNS record, that 'dangling' record quietly becomes exploitable the moment someone else is able to claim that same resource name.
items.impact: The attacker fully controls what is served from an address that looks, to any visitor or automated system, like the organisation's own subdomain. That makes for very convincing phishing hosted on a trusted domain. It also allows theft of cookies scoped to the parent domain, and it defeats any control that trusts that domain — email filters, content security policies, and OAuth redirect allowlists included.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all subdomains for the target's registered domains (via certificate-transparency logs, DNS brute-forcing, or an asset inventory if available) and resolve each to identify its current CNAME/A record target.

Cross-reference each CNAME target against a known-fingerprint database of cloud-provider "resource not found"/"this app doesn't exist" error pages (Subjack, can-i-take-over-xyz maintain such lists) to identify records pointing at a currently-nonexistent resource.

For each candidate, independently verify the dangling state by directly querying the target cloud resource's own status/existence check (not just the fingerprint match) to rule out false positives from a temporarily-unavailable but still-owned resource.

Prioritize findings by the subdomain's apparent trust level (a bare marketing subdomain vs. one referenced in email SPF/DKIM, OAuth redirect URIs, or CSP allowlists) since exploitability impact varies significantly by context.
Confirm the dangling DNS record still resolves to a provider resource that has been released, since a record pointing at a live resource is not takeable.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes claiming/registering the dangling cloud resource, since this step involves creating an account or resource with a cloud provider outside the client's own tenancy, which needs clear authorization and a plan for safe, prompt teardown.
Verify the DNS record is genuinely dangling (points to a resource confirmed not to exist) using the cloud provider's own status check before attempting to claim it.

Register/claim the target resource name with the relevant cloud provider using a test/throwaway account, and confirm that the organization's existing DNS record now resolves to content the tester controls.
Serve a clearly-labeled, benign proof-of-concept page (not a functional phishing page) at the claimed resource to demonstrate the takeover without creating a genuinely deployable phishing artifact.

Immediately release/delete the claimed resource once the finding is documented, and advise the client to remove the dangling DNS record without delay given how easily this could be re-claimed by an unauthorized third party in the interim.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate subdomains and resolve CNAME targets
Check for known dangling-CNAME fingerprints
Manually confirm a candidate's dangling status against the provider directly
examplePayloads.command: curl -sI https://<dangling-target>.s3.amazonaws.com/  # or the equivalent status endpoint for the specific cloud provider/service implicated

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate the zone's records and flag any pointing at released provider resources

variants: Dangling record pointing at a deprovisioned PaaS app (Azure Web Apps, Heroku) versus a deprovisioned storage bucket or CDN distribution — the claiming mechanism differs by provider/service.
Dangling record referenced in an OAuth application's redirect-URI allowlist, enabling token theft via authorization-code interception rather than just simple content spoofing.
A takeover of a subdomain used for email or SSO rather than a web page, which extends the impact from content spoofing to credential interception.
mitigation: Integrate DNS-record cleanup into the resource-decommissioning process itself (a single workflow/checklist step, or better, automated via infrastructure-as-code teardown) so the two never drift out of sync.
Periodically scan the organization's own DNS zone for dangling records pointing at nonexistent cloud resources, using the same fingerprinting approach an external attacker would use.
Where a subdomain is only needed temporarily, use a short TTL and a documented expiry/review date rather than leaving records indefinitely after the underlying resource is gone.
Restrict which subdomains are trusted in security-sensitive contexts (OAuth redirect URIs, CSP allowlists, SPF/DKIM) to only actively-maintained, monitored hostnames.
items.mitigationClientFacing: One of your DNS entries still points to a cloud resource you no longer own, which means someone else can claim that resource and, through it, serve content or receive traffic under your own domain name. Because it is your name, anything they put there inherits your users' trust. This is a housekeeping failure rather than a break-in: the fix is to remove DNS entries whenever the resource they point to is decommissioned, and to review existing entries for any that now point at nothing. Where the affected name is used for email or sign-in, the priority rises sharply, because the takeover then intercepts rather than merely misleads.

items.title: Insecure CI/CD Pipeline OIDC Trust Misconfiguration
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target's CI/CD pipeline configuration (a GitHub Actions workflow file, GitLab CI config, or equivalent) if performing a white-box review, or the ability to submit a workflow run from a forked/attacker-controlled repository if testing black-box from an authorized external repository. Familiarity with OIDC federated-identity trust-policy syntax for the relevant cloud provider (AWS IAM, Azure AD, GCP Workload Identity Federation).
items.whatItIs: Modern CI/CD pipelines (like GitHub Actions) authenticate to the cloud using short-lived tokens instead of permanent passwords — the cloud trusts a token based on details like which repository, branch, or workflow generated it. If those trust conditions are set too loosely — trusting any repository in the org, any branch instead of just the main one, or any workflow — an attacker who can trigger a workflow run somewhere less trusted (a fork, a random feature branch) can get a valid token and take on the same cloud access meant only for the real deployment pipeline.
items.rootCause: These trust conditions are often configured loosely, frequently copied straight from a vendor's quick-start guide that favors broad settings to make initial setup easier. Instead of locking the trust down to the exact repository, branch, and workflow file that should be allowed, it's left open much wider than the pipeline actually needs.
items.impact: An attacker who can trigger a workflow run in a context the trust policy does not properly restrict gets that workflow to assume the cloud role. They might do this by opening a pull request from a fork, or pushing to a branch that is not tightly controlled. The workflow then inherits whatever that role grants, which is frequently broad deployment or infrastructure permissions. The result is a full cloud account compromise that began as an ordinary CI/CD integration.
stepsToIdentify: Review the cloud-side OIDC trust policy (the AWS IAM role's trust relationship, Azure AD federated credential, or GCP Workload Identity Federation provider/pool binding) for the exact claim conditions enforced — subject (repo/branch/workflow), audience, and issuer.
Check whether the trust policy scopes the `sub` claim down to a specific repository AND branch/ref AND workflow file, versus a broad wildcard match at the organization or repository level only.

Determine whether the CI/CD platform's workflow-trigger configuration allows execution from forks or external pull requests, since that's the most common vector for an attacker to obtain a token under a less-trusted context.

Where white-box access to the pipeline configuration isn't available, attempt (with authorization) to trigger a workflow from a fork/feature branch and inspect whether the resulting OIDC token successfully assumes the target cloud role.
Establish how tightly the pipeline's federated trust is scoped — to a specific repository, branch and workflow — since a broadly scoped trust can be assumed from an unrelated repository.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes triggering CI/CD workflow runs from a forked repository or alternate branch/workflow as part of testing the trust-policy boundary.
Identify the exact cloud role the legitimate deployment workflow assumes, and the OIDC claim conditions currently configured to trust it.

Trigger a workflow run from a context the trust policy should not (in principle) trust — a fork, a non-production branch, or a differently-named workflow file that nonetheless matches the loose condition.
Within that workflow run, attempt to assume the target cloud role using the resulting OIDC token and confirm success.

Demonstrate impact via a benign, authorized action using the assumed role's permissions (listing resources, a read-only API call) rather than a destructive action, and document the exact trust-policy condition that was insufficiently restrictive.

examplePayloads.label: Inspect an AWS IAM role's OIDC trust policy for overly broad conditions
Trigger a workflow from a fork to obtain an OIDC token under a broader trust condition
examplePayloads.command: # in the forked repo's workflow YAML: use actions/github-script or aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume set to the target role ARN, then trigger via a pull_request event

examplePayloads.label: Attempt to assume the target role using the resulting OIDC token
Inspect the trust policy's federated conditions for an overly broad subject claim

variants: Trust policy scoped to the correct repository but not the correct branch/ref, allowing any branch (including attacker-created feature branches) to assume the role.
Trust policy scoped correctly for repository/branch but not the specific workflow filename, allowing a new, attacker-added workflow file on an already-trusted branch to assume the role.
A trust condition matching any branch rather than the protected one, allowing a pull-request branch to assume a production deployment role.
mitigation: Scope OIDC trust-policy conditions as tightly as possible: the specific repository, the specific branch/ref (e.g. `refs/heads/main` only), and, where the platform's token claims support it, the specific workflow filename.
Disable workflow execution from forks/external pull requests for any workflow that has access to cloud-deployment secrets or federated roles.
Apply least privilege to the cloud role itself, scoping its permissions to only what the specific deployment task requires, so even a successful trust-policy bypass has bounded impact.
Periodically audit OIDC trust-policy configurations against the vendor's current hardening guidance, since default/quick-start examples are commonly broader than production best practice.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your build-and-deploy pipeline is trusted to obtain cloud credentials automatically, but that trust is scoped too loosely, so a build triggered from an unexpected place — a different branch, a proposed change, in some cases a different repository — can obtain the same production credentials. That turns your automation into a route an attacker can borrow. The fix is to narrow the trust so it applies only to the specific repository, branch and workflow that genuinely deploys, and to nothing else. This is a configuration correction on the trust relationship and is worth prioritising, because it grants production access rather than merely information.

links: CWE-290 (Authentication Bypass by Spoofing)

items.title: Insecure Default VPC Configuration Left Active
items.prerequisites: Read-only access to the target cloud account's networking configuration (VPC/security-group console or CLI access) for a white-box review, or network scanning tools (nmap) if testing black-box against IP ranges known to belong to the target's default VPC.
items.whatItIs: Every new AWS account comes with a default network setup that allows all outbound traffic (and sometimes overly broad inbound access too), with subnets that are all reachable from the internet. This finding is about production systems still running directly inside that default setup instead of a properly designed, more restrictive network.
items.rootCause: The default network exists purely so a brand-new account can launch a server immediately with zero setup — it was never meant to be a production-ready security baseline. But because it works right out of the box, teams often just keep using it and never revisit their network design once things are running.
items.impact: Resources launched into the default setup carry a wider network attack surface than they need. Unrestricted outbound traffic makes data exfiltration and command-and-control callbacks straightforward for any compromised instance, and older default security groups have sometimes shipped with overly permissive inbound rules too. The deeper problem is the absence of deliberate segmentation, which makes a compromise much harder to contain to one tier once it happens.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all VPCs in the account and identify which are the provider-created defaults (flagged as such in the console/CLI output) versus custom-created VPCs.
Check whether any production workload (EC2 instances, RDS databases, load balancers) is deployed into a default VPC/default security group rather than a custom, purpose-built network.
Review the default security group's rule set for unrestricted outbound access and any inbound rules beyond what's genuinely required.
Assess whether network segmentation (separate subnets/security groups for web, application, and data tiers) exists at all, or whether everything sits in one flat network regardless of VPC origin.
Determine whether workloads actually run in the default network or merely inherit its permissive rules, since the finding's impact tracks what is exposed through it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cloud network configuration review and, where applicable, an authorized proof-of-concept exfiltration test from a resource in the default VPC.
Identify a resource (a test instance, if none exists in production for this specific test) running within the default VPC/security group.
From that resource, attempt outbound connections to a range of ports/protocols and destinations to confirm the extent of the unrestricted egress.

Where a compromised-instance scenario is being simulated (with authorization), demonstrate an outbound callback or a simulated data-exfiltration channel to a controlled external endpoint as proof of the egress exposure's practical impact.
Document the specific resources found running in the default network configuration and the exact rules that remain overly permissive.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate default VPCs and their security groups
Inspect the default security group's rule set
Test unrestricted outbound access from within the default VPC
List security groups still permitting broad inbound access in the default network

variants: Default VPC still present and in active use for production workloads versus present-but-unused (lower severity, but still worth flagging as a hardening opportunity given it remains a live, exploitable attack surface if ever accidentally used).
Default security group's outbound-everything rule inherited by newly-launched resources by default because no custom security group was specified at launch time.
A default network retained only for a forgotten legacy instance, which becomes the least-monitored entry point precisely because it is assumed unused.
mitigation: Delete the default VPC in every region where it isn't intentionally in use, following the cloud provider's documented process, to remove it as an accidental deployment target entirely.
Design and deploy a custom VPC with least-privilege security groups (explicit allow-lists for required ports/protocols only, no unrestricted outbound rule) for all production workloads.
Segment the network into tiers (web/application/data) with security groups that only permit the specific inter-tier traffic required.
Include default-VPC and default-security-group checks in routine cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning to catch drift or new accounts that haven't been hardened yet.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your cloud account still uses the provider's default network, which comes preconfigured to be permissive so that things work out of the box. Anything running in it inherits those loose rules, often including broad exposure to the internet. Providers ship it this way for convenience, not security, and the expectation is that you replace it. The fix is to move workloads onto a purpose-built network with rules that grant only what is needed, and to remove or lock down the default. Confirm what is actually running in the default network first, since an empty default network is a tidy-up job while a populated one is an exposure.

items.title: Missing MFA Delete on Critical Storage Buckets
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud storage bucket's configuration (via console or CLI, with appropriate authorization) to check versioning and MFA-delete settings. Credentials for a test IAM principal with delete permissions on the bucket, to demonstrate the deletion/overwrite impact if MFA Delete is confirmed absent.
items.whatItIs: S3 (and similar services elsewhere) has an 'MFA Delete' setting that, when turned on, requires a valid multi-factor code — not just normal permissions — before someone can permanently delete data or turn off version history. When this is left off on buckets holding important or compliance-relevant data, anyone with regular delete permissions (including someone using a stolen credential) can permanently destroy that data with no extra barrier at all.
items.rootCause: MFA Delete has to be turned on manually by the account owner. It can only be configured from the command line, using the account's root credentials together with a physical or virtual MFA device. That is enough extra friction that it commonly gets skipped, even on buckets holding backups or audit logs where deletion would be a serious problem.
items.impact: Anyone holding ordinary delete permissions can permanently destroy critical data — backups, compliance logs, financial records — or switch off versioning so nothing can be recovered. That might be a compromised but legitimate credential, an insider with too much access, or an attacker who obtained credentials some other way. Nothing stands between routine API access and irreversible data loss.
stepsToIdentify: Identify buckets holding critical data (backups, audit/compliance logs, financial records) as the priority scope for this check, since MFA Delete is a targeted control for high-value data rather than a universal requirement for every bucket.
Check each identified bucket's versioning and MFA-Delete status via the bucket's versioning configuration API/console.

Cross-reference which IAM principals/roles have delete permissions on the bucket, to assess how broad the population of potential (accidental or malicious) deleters is in the absence of the MFA-Delete barrier.

Review whether any other compensating control (a bucket policy explicitly denying delete actions except from a specific, tightly-controlled principal, or object-lock/legal-hold configuration) offsets the absence of MFA Delete.
Confirm whether versioning is enabled as well, since deletion protection without versioning still permits overwrite-based destruction of the objects.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes a test deletion/version-overwrite demonstration against a non-production copy or a dedicated test object within the target bucket.
Confirm the bucket's MFA-Delete status is disabled via the versioning configuration check.
Using a test IAM principal with ordinary (non-MFA-gated) delete permissions, delete a specific object version (or a dedicated test object created for this purpose) without providing any MFA code.
Confirm the deletion succeeded with no additional authentication challenge, demonstrating the absence of the MFA-Delete barrier in practice, not just in configuration.
Document the specific critical-data buckets found without MFA Delete enabled and the population of principals capable of performing an equivalent deletion.

examplePayloads.label: Check a bucket's versioning and MFA-Delete status
Attempt a test object-version deletion without MFA
Enumerate principals with delete permissions on the bucket (policy review)
Confirm whether deletion protection is configured on the critical bucket

variants: MFA Delete absent on a bucket that also lacks versioning entirely, meaning deletion is not just unauthenticated-by-MFA but also unrecoverable via any version-rollback mechanism.
MFA Delete absent but partially compensated for by S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the same bucket, which independently prevents deletion regardless of MFA-Delete status.
Protection present on the bucket but absent on its replication target, leaving the replicated copy destroyable and defeating the resilience the replica was meant to provide.
mitigation: Enable versioning and MFA Delete on all buckets holding critical, backup, or compliance-relevant data, accepting the operational overhead of root-user/hardware-MFA-gated configuration changes as justified for this class of data.

Where MFA Delete's operational constraints are prohibitive, apply S3 Object Lock (compliance or governance mode) as an alternative or complementary control preventing deletion/overwrite for a defined retention period.
Restrict delete permissions on critical buckets to the smallest possible set of IAM principals via bucket policy, independent of whether MFA Delete is enabled, as defense in depth.
Include MFA-Delete and Object-Lock status checks in routine cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning for all buckets tagged as holding critical/compliance data.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The storage holding your most important data can be permanently deleted without the extra confirmation step that exists to prevent exactly that — whether by an attacker who gains access, or by an administrator's mistake. Enabling the additional deletion safeguard, together with versioning so that a deleted or overwritten object can still be recovered, closes this. Apply it to the replicated copy as well as the primary, since protecting only one of the two leaves the data destroyable through the other. This is a resilience control: it will not stop an intrusion, but it determines whether one becomes recoverable or catastrophic.

links: CWE-284 (Improper Access Control)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (S3 bucket configuration)

items.title: Insecure Container Escape via Privileged Docker Socket Mount
items.prerequisites: A test container/pod deployed in the target environment (or an authorized equivalent test namespace) with the Docker socket mounted, matching the misconfiguration under test. Standard Docker CLI tooling accessible from within the container.
items.whatItIs: A container is set up with access to the host machine's Docker control socket — usually to let it manage other containers or run build tasks. But that socket is essentially a master key for the entire container host. Anything inside the container that can reach it can tell Docker to spin up a brand-new container with full root access to the host's file system — completely escaping the original container's supposed isolation.
items.rootCause: The Docker socket was connected to the container for a real, legitimate reason, such as managing containers from within a build pipeline. What was not recognised is that access to that socket is equivalent to root access on the entire host. There is no boundary between being able to talk to Docker and being able to do anything Docker can do, including mounting the host's file system.
items.impact: This is a complete compromise of the underlying host. An attacker who can run code inside the container can start a new container with the host's root filesystem attached. That gives them root-equivalent access to the host itself, and from there to every other container and workload running on it.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate running containers/pods and their volume mounts, flagging any with `/var/run/docker.sock` (or the containerd/CRI-O equivalent socket) mounted from the host.
From within a flagged container, check whether the Docker CLI or a raw socket-communication tool is available (or can be installed/copied in) to interact with the mounted socket.
Confirm the socket is genuinely reachable and responsive by issuing a benign, read-only Docker command (e.g. listing running containers) through it.

Assess whether any compensating control (a security profile like AppArmor/SELinux specifically restricting socket use, or a read-only mount) meaningfully limits what can be done via the socket despite its presence.
Confirm the container can reach the host control socket, since that reachability rather than the container's own privilege is what enables the escape.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes container-escape testing against the specific test container/pod with the mounted socket.
From within the container, confirm connectivity to the mounted Docker socket using a benign command.
Issue a command via the socket to launch a new, privileged container with the host's root filesystem (`/`) bind-mounted into it.
From within the newly-launched privileged container, confirm root-equivalent access to the host filesystem (e.g. reading a host file only root should be able to access) as proof of the escape.
Document the exact escape command sequence and the resulting host-level access achieved, then tear down any test containers created during the demonstration.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the Docker socket is mounted and reachable from inside the container
Escape by launching a new privileged container with the host filesystem mounted
examplePayloads.command: docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run -v /:/host --rm -it alpine chroot /host sh

examplePayloads.label: Confirm host-level access from within the escaped container
examplePayloads.command: cat /host/etc/shadow  # proof-of-concept read of a host file only root should access, in an authorized test only

examplePayloads.label: Confirm from inside a container whether the host control socket is mounted and reachable

variants: Escape via the containerd or CRI-O socket rather than the classic Docker daemon socket, relevant to Kubernetes clusters not using Docker as the container runtime directly.
Escape via an overly permissive Kubernetes hostPath volume mount pointing at the socket path, rather than a direct Docker `-v` mount in a non-orchestrated container.
Escape via a hostPath mount of a sensitive host directory rather than the control socket, which achieves host access without the socket being present at all.
mitigation: Never mount the Docker/container-runtime socket into application containers; where dynamic container orchestration is genuinely required, use a properly-scoped, non-root-equivalent API (a dedicated build-orchestration service with its own least-privilege permission model) instead.

If socket access is unavoidable for a specific, well-understood use case, isolate that workload on a dedicated, tightly-monitored host rather than a shared multi-tenant node, and apply a restrictive security profile (AppArmor/SELinux) limiting which socket operations are permitted.
Use rootless container runtimes where feasible, which eliminate the root-equivalence of socket access entirely.
Include Docker-socket-mount detection in routine container security scanning (both static manifest review and runtime admission control) to prevent this misconfiguration from reaching production.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A container in your environment can reach the control channel of the machine hosting it, which lets whatever runs in that container take over the host and, with it, every other container on the same machine. Containers are meant to be isolated from their host; this configuration removes that isolation. The fix is to stop exposing the host's control channel to containers and to run them without the elevated access that makes this reach possible. This matters because it converts a foothold in one small, low-value container into control of the whole host, which is a large step up in an attacker's position.

links: CWE-269 (Improper Privilege Management)
CIS Docker Benchmark

items.title: Insecure Kubernetes Pod Security Standards (Privileged Containers Allowed)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target Kubernetes cluster's Pod Security Standard/Pod Security Policy configuration (or the ability to submit a test pod manifest, with authorization). kubectl configured against a test namespace in the target cluster.
items.whatItIs: The Kubernetes cluster's security settings allow pods to run with full host-level privileges. That includes unrestricted root access, direct access to the host's network or process list, and dangerous low-level system capabilities. Stricter settings would normally block a pod like that from even starting, but they are not being enforced here.
items.rootCause: The cluster's security enforcement was left at its loose default, or was never explicitly locked down to the stricter setting. This commonly happens because one early workload genuinely needed elevated privileges during initial setup, and rather than granting that one exception narrowly, the whole cluster or namespace was left permissive for everything, indefinitely.
items.impact: Any workload running as a privileged pod effectively has root on the underlying node. That includes a workload compromised through an unrelated application flaw. From the node an attacker can reach the host filesystem, other pods' resources, and the node's own credentials and service account tokens. Depending on what those reach, it can extend to the whole cluster.
stepsToIdentify: Check the Pod Security Standards enforcement level applied to each namespace (via the `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` label) or, for clusters still using the deprecated PSP, review the bound PodSecurityPolicy objects.
Enumerate existing running pods for any already configured with `privileged: true`, `hostPID`, `hostNetwork`, or a sensitive `hostPath` mount, using kubectl.
Where authorized, attempt to submit a test pod manifest requesting `privileged: true` in a namespace believed to be permissive, and confirm whether the admission controller accepts or rejects it.

If a privileged pod is confirmed to be schedulable, assess what's reachable from the node itself (other pods' service-account tokens, the kubelet API, cloud-provider instance-metadata service) to size the realistic escalation path.
Establish which namespaces permit privileged pods, since a single permissive namespace undermines the isolation of the whole cluster.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes deploying a privileged test pod into the target cluster/namespace.
Submit a test pod manifest requesting `privileged: true` and a hostPath mount of the node's root filesystem, and confirm the admission controller accepts it.
From within the running privileged test pod, mount and access the node's root filesystem to confirm host-level access.

From the node-level vantage point, attempt to locate and read other pods' mounted service-account tokens or reach the cloud-provider instance-metadata service as a demonstration of lateral-movement potential.
Document the exact admission-control gap (missing or misconfigured Pod Security Standard) and the resulting node/cluster access achieved, then delete all test pods/resources created.

Enumerate existing privileged pods across the cluster
Submit a test privileged pod with a hostPath mount
examplePayloads.command: kubectl apply -f privileged_test_pod.yaml  # spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged: true, hostPath volume mounting '/'

examplePayloads.label: Confirm host filesystem access from within the privileged test pod

variants: Pod granted specific dangerous capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, NET_ADMIN) individually rather than the blanket `privileged: true` flag, achieving similar or partial escalation depending on the specific capability.
Pod with `hostNetwork: true` allowing it to see and interact with all host network traffic and services, distinct from the filesystem/privilege-escalation angle of a fully privileged pod.
A pod that is not privileged outright but requests a single powerful capability, which achieves node compromise while passing a coarse privileged-only check.
mitigation: Enforce the Restricted Pod Security Standard cluster-wide (or at minimum Baseline, with documented, narrowly-scoped exceptions for the specific workloads that genuinely require elevated privileges).
Replace any workload's reliance on `privileged: true` with the specific, minimal Linux capabilities it actually needs, granted individually rather than as a blanket privilege escalation.
Isolate any workload that must remain privileged onto dedicated, tainted nodes separate from general-purpose workloads, limiting the blast radius of a compromise.
Use policy-as-code admission controllers (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) to enforce and continuously audit Pod Security Standard compliance beyond the built-in labels alone.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your container platform allows workloads to run with elevated privileges that let them break out of their isolation and take control of the machine underneath. Individual containers are supposed to be contained; permitting privileged ones removes the wall between a container and its host. The fix is to enforce a policy that forbids privileged workloads and grants each only the narrow capabilities it genuinely needs, applied across every namespace rather than only the obvious ones. A single namespace left permissive undermines the isolation of the entire cluster, so the control has to be comprehensive to be worth anything.

items.title: Cloud Cost Anomaly Indicating Cryptomining Compromise
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's billing/cost-explorer console or API, and, where a compromise is suspected/confirmed, access to compute/container resource inventories to identify the specific abused instance(s).
items.whatItIs: An unexplained, sustained jump in cloud spending — unusual CPU/GPU usage on servers that shouldn't need it, unexpected resources spun up in regions the company doesn't normally use, or billing charges for things nobody provisioned. Investigating usually reveals unauthorized cryptocurrency-mining software running on compromised cloud resources, rather than any real business workload.
items.rootCause: Whatever the attacker used to get in initially — a leaked credential, an exploited app bug, an over-permissioned account — was followed by them installing mining software, which is typically the fastest way to squeeze money out of stolen cloud access. This is usually spotted through the unusual billing pattern it creates, not through any single, specific technical flaw — this finding is really about whether the organization can detect and respond to that pattern, not one root cause.
items.impact: The financial loss is direct and grows for as long as the mining goes unnoticed. Real incidents have run into hundreds of thousands of dollars before anyone spotted them. The more important point is what the cost signals: whatever initial access allowed the mining deployment almost certainly grants the attacker reach into sensitive data and systems too. The bill is usually the first visible symptom of a much larger compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Review the cloud account's cost-explorer/billing dashboard for unexplained spend spikes, particularly compute/GPU line items disproportionate to known, budgeted workloads.
Cross-reference the spend spike's timing and affected region/service against the organization's change-management records to rule out a legitimate, undocumented workload before assuming compromise.

For confirmed anomalies, identify the specific instances/containers responsible via cost-allocation tags or resource-level billing breakdowns, then inspect those resources directly for cryptomining process indicators (unusual outbound connections to known mining-pool domains/IPs, high sustained CPU utilization with no corresponding legitimate workload).

Trace back from the compromised resource to the initial-access vector (a leaked credential, an exploited public-facing vulnerability, an overly permissive IAM role) to scope the full extent of the compromise beyond just the mining activity itself.
Correlate the spend anomaly with the specific service and region, since compute cost concentrated in an unusual region is a stronger cryptomining signal than an overall rise.
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through billing/monitoring review rather than actively exploited by the tester; where a real, live compromise is suspected during an engagement, treat it as an incident requiring immediate escalation to the client rather than a standard test-and-report finding.

If simulating this scenario for a readiness assessment (with explicit authorization), deploy a benign, clearly-labeled CPU-intensive test workload on a designated test instance and confirm whether the client's cost-monitoring/alerting correctly flags the resulting spend anomaly within an acceptable time window.
Assess whether any automated response capability exists (e.g. an alert triggering automatic instance isolation or termination) versus purely manual, delayed human review of billing dashboards.
Document the detection latency observed and any gaps in cost-anomaly alerting coverage (e.g. certain regions/services not included in the monitored scope) as the primary deliverable for this finding.
Confirm the workload driving the cost is unauthorised rather than a legitimate scaling event before treating it as a compromise, by tracing it to a change record or owner.

examplePayloads.label: Review cost-explorer data for anomalous compute spend by service/region
examplePayloads.command: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-06-01,End=2026-07-01 --granularity DAILY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE

examplePayloads.label: Identify high-CPU instances for further inspection
examplePayloads.command: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization --statistics Average --period 3600 --start-time <start> --end-time <end> --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=<instance-id>

examplePayloads.label: Check for connections to known mining-pool infrastructure from a suspect instance
examplePayloads.command: netstat -antp | grep -E ':3333|:4444|:5555|:7777|:8080'  # common mining-pool stratum ports, correlate destination IPs against threat-intel feeds

examplePayloads.label: Break down recent spend by service and region to locate the anomaly
examplePayloads.command: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=<start>,End=<end> --granularity DAILY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=REGION

variants: Cryptomining deployed via a compromised serverless/function-as-a-service resource rather than a persistent VM, producing a different billing signature (per-invocation cost spikes rather than sustained instance CPU cost).

Cryptomining deployed within a compromised container in a shared Kubernetes cluster, where the cost signature may be masked within aggregate cluster billing unless per-namespace cost allocation is in place.
Cost abuse spread deliberately thin across many accounts in an organisation to stay under each account's individual billing alert threshold.
mitigation: Enable and tune cloud-provider cost-anomaly-detection features (AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, Azure Cost Management anomaly alerts, GCP Cost Anomaly Detection) with alerting routed to a team that can respond promptly, not just a monthly billing review.
Apply resource quotas and budget alerts at the account/project/namespace level so an unexpected spend spike triggers an actionable alert well before it accumulates into a large loss.

Address the underlying initial-access vector as the actual security fix — the cost anomaly is a symptom; the credential leak, vulnerable application, or overly permissive IAM policy that enabled the compromise is the root cause requiring remediation.
Restrict which principals/roles can launch new compute resources or modify instance types/counts, reducing the blast radius available to a compromised credential.
items.mitigationClientFacing: An unusual and sustained rise in your cloud costs is a reliable early sign of compromise: once an attacker has access, the most common thing they do is run up large compute bills mining cryptocurrency at your expense. The cost anomaly is often noticed before any security alert. The response is twofold — investigate unexplained spend as a potential incident rather than only a billing question, and set spending alerts that reach someone quickly so the window of abuse is short. Confirm the cause before acting, since a legitimate scaling event looks similar, but treat an unexplained, region-specific surge as suspicious until shown otherwise.

reference.standard: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
tools: AWS Cost Explorer / Cost Anomaly Detection
links: MITRE ATT&CK T1496 (Resource Hijacking)
CWE-284 (Improper Access Control) — for the underlying initial-access vector

items.title: Insecure Cloud Load Balancer Listener Without TLS
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target cloud load balancer's public endpoint. A packet-capture tool (Wireshark/tcpdump) or a network intercepting proxy, and basic port-scanning tooling (nmap) to identify which listener ports are configured without TLS.
items.whatItIs: A cloud load balancer has a listener set up on an unencrypted port (plain HTTP instead of HTTPS) carrying traffic that should be encrypted, instead of enforcing HTTPS everywhere or at least automatically redirecting anyone who hits the plain HTTP port over to the secure one.
items.rootCause: The plain-HTTP listener was probably set up early on to redirect to HTTPS, or is a leftover from an earlier, less careful configuration. Either the redirect was never actually added, or a specific app or API path remains directly reachable over the unencrypted listener with no HTTPS-only rule covering it. Anyone can therefore communicate with it in plain, readable text.
items.impact: Anyone able to observe the network path can read everything sent over the plaintext listener, including credentials, session cookies and application data. They might be on a shared network, on a compromised router in between, or positioned on the local segment. Because unencrypted traffic carries no integrity protection either, they can also modify responses rather than only reading them.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the load balancer's configured listeners and their protocols/ports via the cloud provider's console or CLI.

For any listener found on a plaintext protocol/port, test directly whether it serves application content over that plaintext connection or correctly issues an HTTP 301/302 redirect to the HTTPS equivalent.

Where a redirect is present at the root path, test additional specific application/API paths directly over the plaintext listener to confirm the redirect is applied universally rather than only at the root.
Capture a sample request/response over the plaintext listener (where content is served directly) to document the specific sensitive data exposed as impact evidence.
Confirm whether the plaintext listener is the only one or coexists with an encrypted listener that traffic could be redirected to.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes plaintext-listener traffic capture and interaction testing against the target load balancer.
Connect directly to the plaintext listener port and issue a request to a representative application path.
Capture the resulting traffic and confirm whether content is served in cleartext or a redirect to HTTPS occurs.

If content is served in cleartext, perform a normal application action (a test login, an API call with a test account) over the plaintext connection and capture the resulting sensitive data as proof of concept.
Document every listener/port found serving cleartext content and the specific application paths affected.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate load balancer listeners and protocols
Test whether the plaintext listener serves content directly or redirects
Capture cleartext traffic for a specific application path served over the plaintext listener
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 host <load-balancer-ip> and port 80 -w plaintext_lb_capture.pcap

examplePayloads.label: List the load balancer's listeners and flag any serving plaintext

variants: Redirect correctly applied at the load balancer level for HTTP paths, but a separate raw TCP listener (e.g. for a custom protocol/API) left without any TLS termination at all.

TLS termination present at the load balancer but the backend connection from load balancer to origin server travels in cleartext within the internal network (overlaps with the missing-encryption-between-microservices finding).
A plaintext listener retained for a health-check or redirect that also carries application traffic, so the exposure is wider than the configuration's stated purpose.
mitigation: Configure every client-facing listener to use HTTPS/TLS termination, and configure any remaining plaintext listener to issue an unconditional redirect to its HTTPS equivalent for all paths, not just the root path.
Enable HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) on the HTTPS listener so clients that have previously connected won't be tricked into a plaintext connection even if a redirect is somehow bypassed.

Use a current, strong TLS policy (minimum TLS 1.2, preferably 1.3, with modern cipher suites) on the HTTPS listener, and periodically re-verify the configuration hasn't drifted back to a weaker default.
Include listener-protocol checks in routine cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning across all load balancers in the account.
items.mitigationClientFacing: One of your internet-facing load balancers accepts unencrypted connections, so data passing through it — potentially including credentials — travels in a form anyone positioned on the network can read. The fix is to serve only encrypted connections and to redirect any unencrypted request to the secure equivalent rather than serving it. Check every listener the load balancer offers, not just the main one, since a plaintext listener kept for a health check or a redirect frequently carries real application traffic too. This is a direct exposure of data in transit and should be straightforward to close on infrastructure you already operate.

links: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (ELB/ALB TLS configuration)
OWASP WSTG-CRYP-01 (Testing for Weak Transport Layer Security)

items.title: Missing Encryption in Transit Between Cloud Microservices
items.prerequisites: Network access within the target cloud environment's internal network (a compromised or authorized test instance/pod within the same VPC/cluster) sufficient to observe east-west traffic between microservices. A packet-capture tool (tcpdump/Wireshark) positioned on or near the internal traffic path.
items.whatItIs: Internal services within the same cloud environment talk to each other over plain, unencrypted connections instead of HTTPS, based on the common (but flawed) assumption that traffic staying entirely inside the cloud's internal network is automatically safe since it never touches the public internet.
items.rootCause: Internal traffic between services got deprioritized for encryption compared to traffic facing the internet, based on the assumption that the internal network boundary alone is enough protection. That assumption falls apart the moment any other tenant, a compromised neighboring service, or a malicious insider gets a foothold anywhere on that same internal network — at that point, internal traffic is exactly as easy to intercept as external traffic would be.
items.impact: An attacker who compromises any single workload, or gains any foothold inside the internal network, can read all traffic between services in cleartext. They might arrive through an unrelated vulnerability, a misconfigured shared resource, or lateral movement from a less sensitive service. Internal API credentials, session tokens and data passed between services are all exposed, which turns one limited compromise into broad internal visibility.
stepsToIdentify: Map the microservice architecture's internal communication paths (via service-mesh configuration, network diagrams, or direct observation of DNS/service-discovery records) to identify which services communicate with which.
From an internal vantage point (a test pod/instance within the same network segment), capture traffic between at least two microservices during normal operation.

Inspect the capture for plaintext HTTP versus HTTPS/TLS handshake traffic, and, where a service mesh is in use, check whether mutual TLS (mTLS) is enforced by the mesh's policy configuration versus merely available-but-optional.
Where cleartext traffic is confirmed, identify what sensitive data (internal API keys, session tokens, PII passed between services) is observable.
Establish whether encryption is absent on the internal service path specifically, since perimeter encryption often masks plaintext traffic between services behind it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes internal-network traffic capture from the designated test vantage point within the target environment.
Position the capture tool on or adjacent to the internal traffic path between two identified microservices.
Trigger normal inter-service communication (via a representative end-to-end application action) and capture the resulting traffic.
Extract and document any sensitive data observed in cleartext as proof of the exposure's practical impact.

Where a service mesh is present, additionally check its mTLS enforcement mode (strict vs. permissive) since permissive mode still allows plaintext connections to succeed even if mTLS is technically "enabled."

examplePayloads.label: Capture internal east-west traffic between two services
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 host <service-b-internal-ip> and port <service-b-port> -w internal_traffic.pcap

examplePayloads.label: Inspect the capture for cleartext HTTP versus TLS
Check a service mesh's mTLS enforcement mode (Istio example)
Capture traffic on the internal service network and confirm whether it is encrypted
examplePayloads.command: # on a permitted host in the service subnet, capture and inspect inter-service traffic for plaintext protocols

variants: Service mesh present with mTLS available but set to PERMISSIVE mode rather than STRICT, allowing plaintext connections to succeed alongside encrypted ones.
No service mesh at all, with services communicating via plain HTTP calls hardcoded to internal DNS names with no encryption layer whatsoever.
Encryption enforced between services but absent on the path to a shared datastore or cache, which carries the same sensitive data unprotected.
mitigation: Enforce mutual TLS (mTLS) for all service-to-service communication via a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) set to strict enforcement mode, or implement TLS termination directly in each service if a mesh isn't in use.
Treat the internal network as untrusted by default (a zero-trust approach) rather than assuming network-perimeter containment is sufficient protection for east-west traffic.
Rotate and scope internal service-to-service credentials/tokens narrowly, so even a successful traffic interception yields limited-scope, short-lived access rather than a broadly reusable credential.
Periodically audit service-mesh policy configuration to confirm strict mTLS enforcement hasn't drifted to permissive mode during routine changes.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Traffic between your internal cloud services travels unencrypted, on the assumption that the internal network is trustworthy. That assumption no longer holds in a cloud environment, where an attacker who gains any foothold can read traffic moving between services — including sensitive data and credentials — without further effort. The fix is to encrypt service-to-service traffic, not only the connections at the perimeter. Pay particular attention to the paths to shared databases and caches, which carry the same sensitive data and are the most commonly overlooked. This is defence in depth: it limits how far an initial intrusion can spread.

links: CWE-300 (Channel Accessible by Non-Endpoint)
NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture)

items.title: Overly Permissive Service Account Key Distribution
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's IAM/service-account configuration and, where reviewing distribution practices, access to the organization's code repositories, CI/CD systems, and internal documentation/wikis (with appropriate authorization) to trace where service-account keys have been shared or embedded.
items.whatItIs: Long-lived cloud credentials — AWS access keys, a Google service account key file — get shared widely and left lying around. They end up checked into a repository's history, pasted into chat or email, embedded as plain text in a build pipeline, or downloaded onto multiple engineers' laptops. The alternative is tight control, or replacing them entirely with short-lived, auto-rotating credentials wherever possible.
items.rootCause: A static, downloadable key file is simply the fastest way to get a script or pipeline authenticated. But once that key file exists, it tends to spread — copied into a repo for convenience, shared with a teammate, pasted into a support ticket — with nothing forcing its use to stay controlled or its copies to stay tracked. The credential ends up only as safe as the least careful person who's ever handled a copy of it.
items.impact: A widely distributed static key only has to leak from one of its many locations — a public repository, a compromised laptop, an exposed build log. Whoever finds it gains the full scope of that service account's permissions. Because static keys are routinely forgotten and never rotated, that access often persists for a long time. It also makes incident response harder, since working out which of the many copies leaked can be genuinely difficult.
stepsToIdentify: Search source-control history (including deleted files and prior commits, not just the current HEAD) across the organization's repositories for patterns matching cloud service-account key formats (AWS AKIA-prefixed keys, GCP service-account JSON structure).
Review CI/CD pipeline configuration for service-account keys stored as plaintext environment variables/config rather than referenced from a proper secrets-management integration.
Interview the platform/DevOps team on how many individuals or systems currently hold a copy of any given service-account key, and how key rotation (if any) is tracked.
Cross-reference IAM/service-account last-used timestamps against key age to identify old, rarely-rotated keys that have nonetheless been broadly distributed over their lifetime.
Determine how the service-account key is distributed and how many principals hold it, since a long-lived key shared widely cannot be attributed or cleanly revoked.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes credential-exposure searches across the organization's source control, CI/CD configuration, and documentation systems.
Run an automated secret-scanning tool (gitleaks, truffleHog) across full repository history to identify any committed service-account key material.
Where a live, valid key is discovered via this search, validate its scope of access using a minimal, read-only API call (e.g. an identity/permissions check) rather than a broader action.
Trace the discovered key back to its originating service account and assess what permissions it holds and what resources it can access.
Document every distribution point found (repository, CI/CD config, documentation) for the exposed key, since remediation requires addressing all of them, not just the first one discovered.

examplePayloads.label: Scan full repository history for committed cloud credentials
Validate the scope of a discovered AWS key (read-only check)
Check a discovered key's last-used and age via IAM
List the service account's keys and flag long-lived user-managed ones

variants: Static key exposed in a public (rather than internal-only) repository, which represents immediate, world-readable exposure rather than exposure limited to the organization's own personnel.

Key shared via an ephemeral channel (a chat message, an email) that the organization has no visibility into or retention policy for, making the full extent of its distribution effectively untraceable after the fact.
A key embedded in a container image layer, which persists in the registry and in every derived image long after it is rotated at the source.
mitigation: Eliminate static, long-lived service-account keys wherever a short-lived, automatically-rotated alternative exists (IAM roles with temporary STS credentials for AWS, Workload Identity Federation for GCP, managed identities for Azure).

Where a static key genuinely cannot be avoided, store it exclusively in a dedicated secrets-management service (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager) and reference it at runtime rather than distributing the raw value.
Add automated secret-scanning to the CI/CD pipeline (pre-commit hooks and pipeline-stage scanning) to catch accidental key commits before they reach a shared repository.
Establish and enforce a mandatory key-rotation schedule for any static key that remains in use, and immediately rotate any key confirmed to have been exposed via any distribution point.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Access keys for your cloud service accounts are distributed too widely and live too long, so more people and systems hold them than should, and a leaked key cannot be cleanly traced or revoked without disruption. A single one of these keys leaking — in a repository, a log, a container image — can grant broad access. The fix is to replace long-lived keys with short-lived, automatically-rotated credentials wherever the platform supports it, and to tightly limit who holds any key that must persist. Keys found embedded in code or images should be rotated on the assumption they are already known.

links: CWE-798 (Use of Hard-coded Credentials)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (IAM key rotation)

items.title: Unencrypted Disk Snapshot Shared Publicly
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's disk-snapshot inventory and sharing permissions (via console or CLI). A separate, attacker-controlled test cloud account to demonstrate cross-account access if full exploitation is authorized.
items.whatItIs: A disk snapshot is a complete copy of a server's entire disk, often including operating system files, application data, and any credentials or keys stored on it. Here its sharing setting is public — or set to anyone with an account, which amounts to the same thing for a determined attacker. It is not encrypted either, so anyone who finds it can read everything on it.
items.rootCause: Snapshots are often created for legitimate backup or migration reasons, and the sharing setting gets opened broadly. Sometimes that is deliberate for a temporary migration need, sometimes accidental from a misunderstood permission option. Either way it tends to stay that way, because snapshot permissions receive far less routine review than more visible resources such as storage buckets.
items.impact: Anyone who finds the public snapshot can copy it and attach it as a disk in their own account. That gives them full offline access to everything the original disk held — operating system configuration, application data, and any credentials, keys or sensitive files the instance ever wrote. They need no credentials for the victim's account at all, and the victim sees nothing, because all the activity happens in the attacker's own environment.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all disk snapshots in the target cloud account and check each one's sharing/permission configuration for public or overly-broad cross-account access.

Cross-reference discovered public snapshots against the cloud provider's own public-snapshot listing/marketplace (where such a listing exists) to confirm real-world discoverability, not just theoretical permission breadth.

For any snapshot confirmed public, check whether it's also encrypted — an encrypted snapshot shared publicly is still a finding (metadata/existence disclosure, and a potential target if the key is ever also exposed) but significantly lower severity than an unencrypted one.
Identify what data/workload the snapshot originated from (via naming conventions or tags) to assess the sensitivity of what's exposed.
Confirm the snapshot is shared publicly rather than with a specific account, since public sharing exposes it to untargeted enumeration.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cross-account snapshot access testing using an attacker-controlled test cloud account.
From the test account, attempt to locate and copy the target snapshot using its public sharing permission.
Create a new volume/disk from the copied snapshot and attach it to a test instance in the attacker-controlled account.

Mount the resulting disk and inspect its contents for sensitive data (credentials, application data, configuration files) as proof of the exposure's impact, without further distributing or retaining the recovered data beyond what's needed as evidence.
Document the exact snapshot, its sharing configuration, and the sensitive data categories confirmed present, then delete the copied snapshot/volume from the test account.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate snapshots and their sharing permissions
Check a specific snapshot's create-volume permission (public sharing indicator)
From a test account: copy the public snapshot and create a volume
List snapshots whose permissions include public access
examplePayloads.command: aws ec2 describe-snapshots --owner-ids self --query 'Snapshots[].SnapshotId' --output text | xargs -n1 -I{} aws ec2 describe-snapshot-attribute --snapshot-id {} --attribute createVolumePermission

variants: Snapshot shared with a specific, deliberately-added external AWS account ID for a legitimate migration purpose, but never subsequently revoked once the migration completed.

Public AMI (machine image) built from a compromised or improperly-sanitized snapshot, which carries the same class of exposure but is distributed via the marketplace rather than the snapshot-sharing mechanism directly.
A snapshot shared with a broad partner account rather than the public, which is overlooked by a public-only scan yet still reaches an untrusted third party.
mitigation: Set disk-snapshot sharing permissions to private by default, and require an explicit, documented, time-bounded exception process for any cross-account sharing need.

Encrypt all disk snapshots by default (many cloud providers now support account-wide default encryption for new snapshots), so even an accidental sharing misconfiguration doesn't expose data directly.

Periodically audit snapshot-sharing permissions across the account as part of routine cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning, since these receive less routine attention than more visible resource types.

Sanitize any snapshot intended for legitimate public distribution (a public AMI, for example) of all credentials/sensitive data before publishing, rather than assuming the underlying disk was already clean.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A snapshot of one of your disks has been shared publicly, which means anyone can copy it and read everything the disk contained at the moment it was taken — data, configuration, and any credentials stored on it. Snapshots are easy to share by accident because the sharing setting is a single toggle and the consequence is invisible from the console afterwards. The fix is to make the snapshot private immediately and to review all snapshots for any others shared publicly or with broad partner accounts. Because the exposed data is a point-in-time copy, assume anything it held is compromised and rotate any credentials among it.

links: CWE-284 (Improper Access Control)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (EBS snapshot encryption/sharing)
