items.title: Exposed Terraform State File with Secrets
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud storage location(s) where Terraform state files might be stored (S3 buckets, Azure Storage, GCS buckets, or a Terraform Cloud/Enterprise workspace), or a bucket-enumeration approach if testing black-box for a publicly-exposed state backend.
items.whatItIs: Terraform state files keep a complete record of every resource Terraform manages — and that includes the plain-text value of any secret ever set through it, like a database password or an API key, because Terraform's state format doesn't automatically encrypt or hide sensitive values.
items.rootCause: Terraform's state file is designed to be a full record of every resource's settings, so it can detect changes and plan future updates — and it stores secret values in plain text within that record unless the team specifically sets up encryption for wherever that state file is stored. Teams often store the state file somewhere convenient (like an S3 bucket) without locking down access to it or turning on encryption, since the state file doesn't look as obviously sensitive as, say, a password file.
items.impact: Anyone who can read the state file obtains every secret Terraform ever set on any managed resource. That is effectively a single comprehensive credential dump for the whole infrastructure. They might get that access through an overly permissive storage bucket, a leaked backend credential, or the file being committed to source control by mistake.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the Terraform backend configuration in use (from the `backend` block in the organization's Terraform code, if accessible) and check the access permissions on the underlying storage location.

If the backend is an S3/GCS/Azure Storage bucket, check whether it's publicly accessible or accessible to a broader set of principals than strictly necessary, using the same techniques as the general publicly-accessible-bucket finding.

Search source-control repositories for accidentally committed `.tfstate` or `.tfstate.backup` files, since local/default backend usage sometimes results in the state file being committed alongside the Terraform code itself.

Where a state file is accessible, search its content directly for common secret-shaped fields (`password`, `secret`, `private_key`, `access_key`) to confirm actual secret presence rather than assuming based on backend exposure alone.
Establish whether the state backend is versioned and access-controlled, since the state file records every resource and frequently embeds secrets in plaintext.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes accessing and inspecting the target Terraform state file/backend.
Access the identified state file via whatever exposure vector was found (an overly permissive bucket, a committed file in source control).
Parse the state file's JSON structure and extract any plaintext secret values present in resource attributes.
Validate the scope of a discovered credential using a minimal, read-only check (e.g. an authentication test) rather than a broader action.
Document every secret type found in the state file and the specific access-control gap that exposed it.

examplePayloads.label: Check a suspected Terraform-backend S3 bucket for public/broad access
Search source control for accidentally committed state files
Extract secret-shaped values from an accessed state file
examplePayloads.command: jq '.. | objects | select(has("password") or has("secret") or has("private_key"))' terraform.tfstate

examplePayloads.label: Confirm whether the state backend bucket restricts access
examplePayloads.command: aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket <state-bucket> && aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket <state-bucket>

variants: State file exposed via source-control commit rather than backend misconfiguration, meaning historical versions may remain accessible even after the current file is removed/gitignored.

State file backend correctly access-controlled, but state-locking/backup copies (a `.tfstate.backup` file, or a versioned prior state in the same bucket) left with different, more permissive access settings.
Secrets exposed not in the remote state itself but in a local state copy left in a repository or a CI artifact, which bypasses the backend's access controls entirely.
mitigation: Store Terraform state exclusively in a properly access-controlled, encrypted-at-rest remote backend (an S3 bucket with a strict bucket policy and default encryption enabled, or Terraform Cloud/Enterprise with its built-in state encryption), never in source control.

Use a secrets-management integration (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) for genuinely sensitive values referenced by Terraform, combined with the `sensitive = true` attribute flag to reduce (though not eliminate, given the state-file limitation) inadvertent exposure in logs/plan output.
Restrict access to the state backend to only the specific CI/CD service principal and a minimal set of authorized engineers, and audit that access list regularly.
Add automated scanning for accidentally committed `.tfstate` files to the same secret-scanning pipeline used for other credential types.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The file your infrastructure tooling uses to track what it has built is stored without adequate protection, and that file records every resource in detail and frequently contains secrets in plain text. Anyone who reads it gains both a map of your environment and, often, working credentials. The fix is to store this file in a properly access-controlled and versioned location, and to keep secrets out of it by referencing a secret store rather than embedding values. Watch for stray copies too — a local copy left in a code repository or a build artifact bypasses the protection on the main one entirely.

links: CWE-798 (Use of Hard-coded Credentials)
HashiCorp Terraform documentation: Sensitive Data in State

items.title: Publicly Accessible Cloud Storage Bucket
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target cloud storage endpoints. A bucket-enumeration tool (S3Scanner, or a manual approach combined with the naming-convention discovery from the related predictable-naming finding) and standard HTTP tooling (curl) to test unauthenticated access directly.
items.whatItIs: A cloud storage bucket's permissions allow 'everyone' — or anyone with any account at all on that cloud platform — to read (and sometimes even write to) it, instead of being limited to specific, named people or systems. That means any random internet user can potentially list and download the bucket's contents directly.
items.rootCause: The bucket's access settings were made public or broadly open, often as a quick fix for a genuine need such as serving public website images, and never narrowed afterwards. In other cases it is an accidental default that slipped through. Bucket permissions tend to get far less scrutiny than more visible application-level access controls.
items.impact: The bucket's contents are readable by anyone, with no authentication, and where writes are also permitted they can be modified or replaced. How serious that is depends entirely on what is actually stored there. It might be harmless static website assets, or it might be customer records, financial data, internal documents or source code. That has to be checked directly — the bucket's name is not a reliable guide.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate candidate bucket names (via OSINT, the predictable-naming approach from the related finding, or a client-provided asset inventory) and test each for public listing/read access.

For each bucket found publicly listable, review the actual object contents (file names, and where appropriate to sample, the content of a representative subset) to assess data sensitivity, rather than stopping at "the bucket is public" as the complete finding.
Test whether write access is also granted (attempt an unauthenticated PUT of a benign test object) to determine if this is a read-only exposure or a full tamper/upload risk as well.

Cross-reference the bucket's actual business purpose (from naming/tags/content) against whether public access was ever a deliberate, appropriate choice (e.g. a bucket genuinely serving public static website assets) versus an unintentional misconfiguration.
Confirm whether public access is granted by the bucket policy, an object ACL, or an account-level setting, since each is remediated in a different place.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated access testing against the target cloud storage buckets.
Attempt unauthenticated listing of the bucket's contents.
If listing succeeds, download a representative, minimal sample of objects (not a bulk exfiltration) sufficient to characterize the data's sensitivity.
Attempt an unauthenticated write of a clearly-labeled, benign test object to check for write-level exposure, then remove it immediately after confirming the result.
Document the bucket's access configuration, the specific data categories confirmed present, and whether read-only or read/write access was achievable.

examplePayloads.label: Test unauthenticated bucket listing
Download a sample object to assess content sensitivity
Test unauthenticated write access with a benign test object
examplePayloads.command: curl -X PUT https://<target-bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/poc-test-object.txt --data 'authorized VAPT test object - safe to delete' -v

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the bucket's effective public-access posture across all four settings
examplePayloads.command: aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket <bucket> && aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket <bucket>

variants: Bucket policy grants access to "any authenticated AWS user" rather than fully anonymous access — a narrower but still very broad exposure, since any individual with any AWS account (trivial and free to create) qualifies.
Bucket itself private but individual object-level ACLs override the bucket default to grant public access on specific objects only.
A bucket private at the policy level but exposing individual objects through per-object ACLs, which a bucket-level check reports as safe.
mitigation: Set the bucket's default access policy to fully private, and enable the cloud provider's account-wide "block public access" setting (AWS S3 Block Public Access) as a safety-net override against any future accidental public-grant attempt.

Where public access to specific content is genuinely required (static website assets), serve it through a CDN/dedicated public-website configuration with a narrowly-scoped bucket policy limited to exactly that content, rather than making the whole bucket public.
Audit both bucket-level and individual object-level ACLs, since a correctly-private bucket policy can still be undermined by a public ACL grant on specific objects.
Include public-bucket detection in continuous, automated cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning rather than relying solely on periodic manual VAPT engagements to catch this drift.
items.mitigationClientFacing: One of your cloud storage containers is readable by anyone on the internet, exposing whatever it holds. This is among the most common and most exploited cloud mistakes, because attackers scan for open containers continuously and the data inside is often sensitive. The fix is to remove public access, but the reason it recurs is that access can be granted in several different places — the container's policy, individual file permissions, or an account setting — so all must be checked. Enabling the provider's account-wide block on public access is the most reliable safeguard, since it overrides the individual settings that get changed by mistake.

links: CWE-668 (Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (S3 public access)

items.title: Cloud API Gateway Throttling Bypass
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target cloud API Gateway endpoint. A scripting/load-testing tool capable of sending requests with varied identifying attributes (Postman/Newman, a custom script using multiple source IPs/API keys/user agents) to test whether throttling is bypassable via attribute manipulation.
items.whatItIs: A cloud API Gateway's rate-limiting is based on something the client can easily change — like just their IP address, without also checking their API key or actual logged-in identity. That means an attacker can bypass the intended limit simply by switching IP addresses.
items.rootCause: Rate limiting was set up using the simplest option available — IP address, since it needs no extra client-identification work — without accounting for how easy it is to rotate IP addresses using proxies, cloud servers, or IPv6 address ranges. A limit based only on IP is far weaker in practice than its configured number suggests.
items.impact: An attacker spreads their requests across many source addresses using a botnet, a pool of cloud instances, or IPv6 rotation. Each individual stream stays under the configured per-IP limit, so the throttle never triggers. The abuse it was built to stop goes ahead at full volume: credential stuffing, brute-force attempts, scraping, or exhausting backend resources.
stepsToIdentify: Review the API Gateway's throttling/rate-limiting configuration to determine exactly which request attribute(s) it keys on (source IP, API key, authenticated identity, or a combination).

With authorization, send a burst of requests from a single source IP to confirm the configured limit does trigger a throttling response (429) at the expected threshold, establishing the baseline is genuinely enforced at all.

Repeat the burst test while varying the keyed attribute (rotating source IP via a proxy pool, or varying a client-supplied header if that's what's keyed on) and observe whether the aggregate request volume across all variations exceeds what a single client should be limited to.

Assess whether any secondary, coarser-grained protection (a global rate limit independent of per-client keying, a WAF rule) provides a compensating backstop even if the primary per-client throttle is bypassable.
Establish whether the throttle is enforced per-key, per-account or globally, since a per-key limit is multiplied simply by acquiring additional keys.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes rate-limit-bypass testing against the target API Gateway endpoint, including sending traffic from multiple source IPs/identities.
Establish the baseline throttling threshold by sending requests from a single, consistent source until a 429 response is observed.

Distribute an equivalent or greater volume of requests across multiple source IPs/keyed-attribute values and confirm whether the aggregate volume succeeds without triggering the same throttling response.

Where the endpoint is authentication-related, demonstrate the practical consequence by running a bounded, authorized brute-force/credential-stuffing simulation against a test account, using the confirmed bypass technique, within an agreed volume/time budget.
Document the exact keyed attribute, the bypass technique used, and the resulting effective rate achieved versus the intended limit.

examplePayloads.label: Baseline burst to confirm throttling triggers on a single source
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 100); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<api-gateway-endpoint>/resource; done

examplePayloads.label: Distributed burst rotating source IP via a proxy pool to test bypass
examplePayloads.command: for proxy in $(cat proxy_list.txt); do curl -s -x $proxy -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<api-gateway-endpoint>/resource; done

examplePayloads.label: Test bypass via a client-supplied header if the throttle keys on that instead of IP
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 100); do curl -s -H "X-Client-Id: client-$i" https://<api-gateway-endpoint>/resource; done

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the effective rate limit by measuring the response to a controlled burst
examplePayloads.command: # issue a bounded burst of authorised requests and record where throttling responses begin

variants: Throttle keyed on a client-supplied header (easily rotated with no infrastructure cost) rather than source IP, making the bypass even simpler than IP rotation.

Throttle correctly keyed on authenticated identity/API key for authenticated endpoints, but a separate, unauthenticated endpoint on the same gateway keyed only on IP, providing an easier bypass path for testing credentials before authentication is even attempted.
A limit enforced at the gateway but bypassed by invoking the backing function directly, where its resource URL is discoverable.
mitigation: Key rate limiting on the most robust available identifier for the endpoint's context — authenticated user/API key where authentication is required, and a combination of IP plus other request-fingerprinting signals for unauthenticated endpoints, rather than IP alone.
Implement a secondary, global/aggregate rate limit independent of per-client keying as a backstop against distributed bypass attempts.

Apply progressive/adaptive throttling that tightens automatically when many distinct keyed-attribute values are observed hitting the same endpoint pattern in a short window, which is itself a signature of a distributed-bypass attempt.
Combine gateway-level throttling with a Web Application Firewall (WAF) capable of behavioral/anomaly-based rate limiting that doesn't rely solely on a single client-supplied attribute.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The control that limits how quickly your cloud service can be called can be circumvented, allowing an attacker to make requests far faster than intended — overloading the service, running up costs, or defeating a protection the limit provided. Often the limit is enforced per access key and can simply be multiplied by using several keys, or is enforced at the gateway but bypassed by calling the underlying service directly. The fix is to enforce the limit per account rather than per key, and to ensure the backing service cannot be reached around the gateway. How serious this is depends on what the throttled action protects.

links: CWE-799 (Improper Control of Interaction Frequency)
OWASP API Security Top 10 - API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption

items.title: Cloud Container Image Vulnerability (Outdated Base Image)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target container registry (or the built images themselves) to pull and scan them. A container image vulnerability scanner (Trivy, Grype, or the cloud provider's native registry scanning feature).
items.whatItIs: Containers running in production are built on an old base image — an outdated Linux version or an old runtime — carrying known, publicly documented security bugs. This happens because the build pipeline pinned a specific version once and never revisited it. Or because it only rebuilds on a schedule too infrequent to pick up new security patches in time.
items.rootCause: Base images get locked to a specific version at first, which is often a reasonable choice for consistency — but there's no follow-up process to bump that version and rebuild whenever the base image gets a security patch upstream. So the pinned version quietly accumulates known, unpatched vulnerabilities the whole time it stays in use.
items.impact: Any known flaw in the outdated base image becomes exploitable against the running container, provided the vulnerable component is actually reachable. That might be a library the application uses directly, or an operating system utility the application never calls but which becomes reachable through another flaw such as command injection. Severity depends on which specific vulnerabilities are present and whether anything can reach them.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the container images currently deployed to production (via the orchestrator's running-pod/task image references) and pull each for scanning.
Run a container-image vulnerability scanner against each image and review the resulting CVE list, prioritizing Critical/High severity findings with a known public exploit.
Cross-reference the base-image tag/digest against the vendor's currently-supported/patched version to quantify how far behind the deployed image has drifted.

For any Critical/High CVE found, assess reachability — whether the vulnerable component is actually invoked by the running application, or present but dormant — to prioritize remediation effort accurately.
Determine whether the vulnerable base image is actually deployed rather than merely present in the registry, since a stored-but-unused image is a lower priority.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes pulling and scanning the target's deployed container images.
Run the vulnerability scanner against each identified image and record the full CVE findings list with severity ratings.
For the highest-severity, most-reachable finding, research whether a public proof-of-concept or exploit exists for that specific CVE.

Where safe and clearly scoped, demonstrate the specific vulnerability against a non-production test deployment of the same image (rather than production) to confirm real-world exploitability rather than relying on the scanner's severity rating alone.
Document the specific base image, its version drift from current, and the prioritized CVE list with reachability assessment for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Scan a container image for known vulnerabilities
Alternative scanner with SBOM generation
Check the base image's tag against current upstream releases
Scan the running image for known-vulnerable components

variants: Vulnerable base OS packages present but not directly reachable by the application (lower practical risk despite a high CVSS score) versus a vulnerable application-runtime library actively used in request-handling code paths.

Vulnerability introduced not by the base image itself but by an outdated application dependency layered on top of an otherwise current base image, requiring dependency-level scanning in addition to base-image scanning.
A vulnerability present only in a build-stage image that is nonetheless pushed to the registry, providing an attacker a vulnerable artifact even though the runtime image is clean.
mitigation: Establish an automated image-rebuild pipeline triggered on a regular schedule (and ideally on upstream base-image security-advisory publication) to keep the pinned base-image version current.

Integrate container-image vulnerability scanning into the CI/CD pipeline as a release gate, failing builds that introduce new Critical/High severity CVEs rather than only discovering them via periodic external scanning.
Prefer minimal base images (distroless, Alpine, or slim variants) to reduce the overall package surface area and corresponding CVE exposure.
Maintain an inventory of base-image versions in use across all deployed images to prioritize remediation efforts and detect drift at a glance.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Some of your running containers are built on outdated base images that contain known, published security flaws, each with a fix already available. Attackers scan for exactly these, because the weaknesses are documented and reliable. The fix is to rebuild on current base images and to make image scanning a routine part of your build process so that outdated components are caught before they are deployed rather than after. Prioritise the images that are actually running over those merely stored, and be aware that a vulnerable build-stage image pushed to your registry is itself an artifact an attacker can use.

links: CWE-1035 (2017 OWASP Top 10 A9 - Using Components with Known Vulnerabilities)
NVD (nvd.nist.gov) for specific base-image CVE lookups

attack.name: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools

items.title: Exposed Cloud Database Snapshot Publicly Shared
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's database-snapshot inventory and sharing permissions (via console or CLI). A separate, attacker-controlled test cloud account to demonstrate cross-account restoration if full exploitation is authorized.
items.whatItIs: A database snapshot — a full point-in-time copy of a database's data — is shared in a way that lets another cloud account (or, worst case, any account at all) restore a brand-new database from it. This sharing setting was left in place after whatever original reason justified it (a migration, a backup strategy) — if there ever was a real reason.
items.rootCause: Database snapshot sharing settings, like disk snapshot settings, live in a separate, less-reviewed place compared to the live database's own access controls. A snapshot can end up shared broadly even when the actual running database is properly locked down, since these two permission systems don't automatically stay in sync — and snapshot sharing is often set up once for a specific need and simply never revisited.
items.impact: Anyone with access to the shared snapshot can restore a complete, fully populated copy of the database into their own account. They then have full access to every record it held at that moment — customer data, financial records, whatever it contained. The live database's network rules and login controls are irrelevant here, because the exposure happens at the snapshot layer instead.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all database snapshots in the target cloud account and check each one's sharing/permission configuration for cross-account or public restoration access.

For any snapshot found shared, determine whether the sharing target is a specific, documented external account (potentially legitimate, but requiring verification it's still needed) or effectively open to any account.
Cross-reference the snapshot's originating database and its business purpose (via naming/tags) to assess the sensitivity of the data it would expose if restored.

Check whether the snapshot is encrypted, and if so, whether the corresponding encryption key is also shared with the same external account(s) — a snapshot shared without its key remains meaningfully protected.
Confirm the database snapshot is shared publicly rather than restored into an isolated account, since public sharing exposes the full dataset to enumeration.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cross-account database-snapshot restoration testing using an attacker-controlled test cloud account.
From the test account, attempt to restore a new database instance from the shared snapshot.

Once restored, connect to the new instance using its default/known credentials (or the credentials embedded in the snapshot's data, if the database engine stores them accessibly) and query a representative, minimal sample of data to confirm sensitivity.
Document the exact snapshot, its sharing configuration, and the confirmed data categories exposed, then delete the restored instance and any copied snapshot from the test account.

Where the snapshot is encrypted, additionally check whether the associated key was also shared, since this determines whether restoration alone is sufficient for exploitation or whether an additional key-sharing gap would need to exist too.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate database snapshots and their sharing attributes
From a test account: restore a database instance from the shared snapshot
Query the restored instance for a representative data sample
List database snapshots whose restore permission includes public access

variants: Automated snapshot sharing configured as part of a cross-region/cross-account disaster-recovery strategy that inadvertently grants broader restoration access than the DR plan actually requires.
Snapshot shared with a specific external account for a one-time migration that has since completed, but the sharing permission was never revoked afterward.
A manual snapshot shared to enable a migration and never un-shared afterwards, which persists as an exposure long past the task it was created for.
mitigation: Set database-snapshot sharing to private by default, and require an explicit, documented, time-bounded exception process for any cross-account sharing need, with a scheduled revocation date.

Encrypt all database snapshots by default, and ensure any legitimate cross-account sharing arrangement also carefully scopes the associated key-sharing to only the specific, necessary external account.

Periodically audit database-snapshot sharing permissions across the account as part of routine cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning, treating it as equally important as live-database access-control review.

Rotate default database credentials on any snapshot/restored instance rather than relying on them remaining secret, since a snapshot's embedded credential state should not be treated as a security boundary.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A snapshot of one of your databases has been shared publicly, which lets anyone restore their own copy and read the entire dataset it contained — every record, as it stood when the snapshot was taken. This is a full data exposure, not a partial one, and it is invisible from your side once shared. The fix is to make the snapshot private immediately and review all database snapshots for others in the same state, including those shared broadly with partner accounts rather than the whole public. Assume the data has been copied and handle it as a disclosure, including any regulatory obligations that follow from what the database held.

links: CWE-284 (Improper Access Control)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (RDS snapshot configuration)

items.title: Exposed Cloud Function Environment Variables
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud function's configuration (console or CLI, with appropriate authorization) or, for a black-box test, any vulnerability in the function's own code (an information-disclosure bug, a debug endpoint) that might reveal its environment variables indirectly.
items.whatItIs: A serverless function stores sensitive settings — database connection details, API keys, third-party credentials — as plain-text environment variables instead of pulling them from a dedicated secrets service. Those environment variables end up visible to anyone with read access to the function's configuration — a much wider group than should actually see the secrets — and sometimes get accidentally logged when the function hits an error.
items.rootCause: Environment variables are the easiest way to hand configuration to a serverless function. During development, the distinction between a harmless setting and a genuinely sensitive secret often is not maintained. Both end up stored the same way, readable by anyone who can view the function's configuration — a much broader group than those who should have access to production secrets.
items.impact: Anyone who can read the function's configuration sees the secrets in plain text, straight from the console or API. That group is often larger than the group trusted with production secrets, since monitoring and deployment tooling legitimately needs configuration access. There is a second path too: if the runtime ever logs its full environment, which happens during debugging or when an unhandled error dumps process state, those secrets spread into log systems with an even wider audience.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the target's serverless functions and, with appropriate authorization, review each one's configured environment variables for secret-shaped values (API keys, connection strings, tokens) rather than genuinely non-sensitive configuration.
Check the IAM/RBAC permission model for who can read function configuration versus who is authorized to access production secrets directly, to assess how much broader the exposed population is.
Review the function's logging configuration and code for any full-environment dump (a debug log statement, an unhandled-exception handler) that could leak the same values into log aggregation.

Check whether a proper secrets-management integration (a Secrets Manager reference, a Key Vault reference) is available and simply unused, versus the platform genuinely lacking such an integration option.
Confirm whether the function's environment variables hold secrets in plaintext rather than references to a managed secret store.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes configuration-read access review and, where applicable, log-content review for the target serverless function.
Read the function's environment-variable configuration directly (via console or API) and extract any secret-shaped values found.
Validate a discovered credential's scope using a minimal, read-only check (e.g. an authentication test against the associated service).
Where log-based leakage is suspected, trigger a benign error condition in a test invocation and check the resulting log entry for full-environment dump content.
Document every secret found, its value's scope of access, and whether it was exposed via direct configuration read, log leakage, or both.

examplePayloads.label: Read a Lambda function's environment variable configuration
Validate a discovered credential's scope (read-only check)
examplePayloads.command: aws sts get-caller-identity --profile discovered-key  # or the equivalent auth-test call for the specific credential type found

examplePayloads.label: Check function logs for an inadvertent full-environment dump
Inspect the function's configured environment for plaintext secrets

variants: Secrets exposed via configuration-read access alone (console/API visibility) versus additionally leaked into log aggregation via a debug statement or unhandled-exception handler.
Secret shared identically across multiple function environment configurations (dev/staging/prod all using the same value), multiplying the impact of a single exposure.
Secrets absent from the environment but written to the function's log output at startup, which relocates the exposure to the log store.
mitigation: Reference genuinely sensitive values from a dedicated secrets-management service (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) at runtime rather than storing them directly as environment variables.

Where the platform supports it, use its native secrets-reference environment-variable feature (which resolves the value at invocation time without exposing it in the plaintext configuration) rather than a raw string value.
Scrub environment-variable content from any log statement, and specifically avoid full-environment dumps in exception handlers.
Restrict configuration-read IAM permissions on functions holding sensitive environment variables to the same narrow population authorized for the secrets themselves.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The configuration values attached to your cloud functions hold secrets — keys, passwords, tokens — in plain text, where anyone able to view the function's settings can read them. These values are easy to inspect and are not designed to hold secrets safely. The fix is to move secrets into a dedicated secret store and have the function retrieve them at runtime, rather than storing them in its configuration. Check the function's logs as well, since a common variant is a secret that has been moved out of the configuration but is still printed to the log when the function starts, relocating rather than removing the exposure.

links: CWE-798 (Use of Hard-coded Credentials)
CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File)

items.title: Exposed Cloud Monitoring/Logging Data Publicly
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target's cloud monitoring/logging dashboard endpoints or storage locations (a public-facing Grafana/Kibana instance, an exposed CloudWatch dashboard, or a log-export bucket). Standard web/HTTP tooling to test unauthenticated access.
items.whatItIs: A monitoring or logging dashboard — like a Grafana or Kibana instance, or a bucket where logs get archived — is reachable from the public internet with no login required at all, exposing application logs, error details, infrastructure metrics, and sometimes accidentally-logged sensitive data to anyone who stumbles onto it.
items.rootCause: Monitoring tools usually get set up quickly to be operational for the internal team. Authentication is either left off or at a default during initial setup and never revisited. Alternatively the dashboard sits on a network segment more broadly reachable than intended. Monitoring infrastructure simply does not receive the security scrutiny given to customer-facing systems.
items.impact: Exposed logs and metrics usually contain far more than the organisation intends to publish. That includes internal hostnames and network layout, and error traces revealing the technology stack and versions in use, which is directly useful for planning further attacks. Not infrequently they also contain credentials, API keys or customer data that ended up in a log line nobody expected to be read outside the team.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the target's known subdomains and infrastructure for common monitoring-tool hostnames/paths (grafana., kibana., a `/logs` or `/metrics` path on an otherwise-known host) using DNS enumeration and web crawling.
For each candidate found, test direct access without providing any credentials and observe whether a login prompt appears or dashboard/log content is served directly.

Where access succeeds, review a representative sample of the exposed data for sensitive content (credentials in logs, PII, internal architecture details) rather than treating exposure alone as the complete finding.

Check whether the exposure is a genuine public-internet reachability issue versus merely an internal-network resource that's incidentally reachable due to the specific vantage point the test was conducted from (clarify network scope before concluding severity).
Establish what the exposed monitoring data contains, since logs frequently include internal hostnames, tokens and request contents beyond the metrics themselves.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes accessing the identified monitoring/logging endpoint(s) without credentials.
Attempt direct, unauthenticated access to each candidate endpoint and confirm which serve content without any login challenge.
Review a representative, minimal sample of the exposed data to characterize its sensitivity (not a bulk download of the full historical log archive).
Where credentials or other genuinely sensitive data are found within the exposed logs, flag them for immediate rotation recommendation as an urgent, separate finding alongside the exposure itself.
Document each exposed endpoint, its content type, and the specific sensitive data categories confirmed present.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate common monitoring-tool subdomains
Test unauthenticated access to a discovered dashboard
examplePayloads.command: curl -sI https://grafana.<target-domain>/  # check for a 200 response serving dashboard content vs. a login redirect

examplePayloads.label: Search accessible log content for inadvertently-logged secrets
Confirm whether the logging destination permits public or broad access

variants: Dashboard itself requires authentication but exposes a separate, unauthenticated API endpoint that serves the same underlying data.
Exported/archived logs stored in a publicly-accessible storage bucket (overlapping with the general publicly-accessible-bucket finding) rather than exposure via a live dashboard interface.
A monitoring dashboard shared by an unauthenticated link rather than an open storage location, which is missed by a storage-focused scan.
mitigation: Require authentication (SSO integration where possible) for all monitoring/logging dashboards and their underlying APIs, with no unauthenticated fallback path.
Restrict network reachability of monitoring infrastructure to internal networks/VPN only, rather than placing it on a publicly-routable endpoint at all.
Implement and enforce log-scrubbing/redaction for known-sensitive field patterns (passwords, API keys, PII) before log data is persisted or indexed, reducing the impact of exposure if it does occur.
Apply the same security scrutiny (periodic access review, network-exposure scanning) to monitoring/logging infrastructure as is applied to customer-facing application infrastructure.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your monitoring or logging data is exposed to broader access than it should be, and that data routinely contains more than metrics — internal system names, request contents, and sometimes tokens or credentials captured in the logs. An attacker reading it gains both intelligence about your environment and, at times, direct access. The fix is to restrict the monitoring and logging destinations to the people and systems that need them, and to be aware that a shared dashboard link can expose the same data as an open storage location. Establishing what the logs actually contain is the first step, since that sets how serious the exposure is.

links: CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File)
OWASP WSTG-CONF-05 (Enumerate Infrastructure and Application Admin Interfaces)

items.title: Exposed CloudFormation/ARM Template with Hardcoded Secrets
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target's infrastructure-as-code repositories (CloudFormation/ARM template source files) or any location these templates might have been inadvertently published (a public repository, an artifact bucket). Standard text-search/secret-scanning tooling.
items.whatItIs: An infrastructure-as-code file (like a CloudFormation or ARM template) used to set up cloud resources has a secret — a database password, an API key, a private key — typed directly into it as plain text, instead of pulling that value securely from a secrets service. And that template itself is stored or shared somewhere it shouldn't be readable from.
items.rootCause: Templates get written for convenience — typing a value directly in is simpler than wiring up a secrets-manager reference during early development — and that habit sticks around even after the template gets checked in and potentially shared widely, with no automated check in the review process catching it before it's committed.
items.impact: Anyone who can read the template gets the credential in plain text. That is typically a wider group than those trusted with production secrets, because infrastructure-as-code repositories are often broadly readable inside an organisation — and occasionally made public by accident. The problem compounds because templates get copied to spin up new environments, so the same hardcoded secret spreads across multiple deployments.
stepsToIdentify: Search the target's infrastructure-as-code repositories (and any public repositories, artifact registries, or documentation where templates might have been shared) for CloudFormation/ARM template files.

Run a secret-scanning tool across the located templates, and separately grep for common secret-parameter patterns (`MasterUserPassword`, `adminPassword`, `ApiKey`) with literal (non-parameterized) values.
For any hardcoded value found, validate whether it's a genuine, live secret (versus an obviously fake/placeholder example value) using a minimal, read-only check where the credential type allows it.

Check whether the template uses the cloud provider's built-in dynamic-reference/parameter mechanism for secrets (CloudFormation dynamic references to Secrets Manager, ARM template Key Vault references) elsewhere in the same codebase, indicating the team is aware of the correct pattern but didn't apply it consistently.
Confirm whether the infrastructure template embeds secrets directly rather than referencing a secret store or parameter.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes searching the target's infrastructure-as-code repositories and any publicly-accessible copies for hardcoded secrets.
Run secret-scanning across all located templates and manually review any close matches the automated scan might miss due to non-standard parameter naming.
For each confirmed hardcoded secret, validate its scope of access with a minimal, read-only check.
Determine whether the same template (and thus the same hardcoded secret) has been reused across multiple environments/deployments, which affects remediation scope.
Document every discovered secret, its location, and its validated scope of access.

examplePayloads.label: Search infrastructure-as-code repositories for hardcoded secrets
Grep specifically for common CloudFormation/ARM secret-parameter patterns with literal values
Validate a discovered database credential (read-only check)
Search the deployed template body for embedded secrets

variants: Secret hardcoded in a template that was never actually deployed (a draft/example template) versus one actively used for live production infrastructure — both are findings, but severity differs based on whether the exposed secret is genuinely live.

Secret hardcoded but the template itself is properly access-restricted internally, with exposure occurring only because a copy was inadvertently published to a public repository or forum for troubleshooting purposes.
A secret absent from the template but passed as a plaintext parameter recorded in the deployment history, which retains it after the template is cleaned.
mitigation: Reference all secrets from a dedicated secrets-management service using the cloud provider's native dynamic-reference mechanism (CloudFormation dynamic references, ARM template Key Vault references) rather than hardcoding literal values in templates.
Add automated secret-scanning to the CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure-as-code repositories specifically, as a release/merge gate rather than a periodic external check.
Rotate any credential confirmed to have been hardcoded in a template, especially if that template was ever published or shared outside its intended internal audience.
Establish and enforce a clear internal standard for infrastructure-as-code secret handling, with example templates demonstrating the correct dynamic-reference pattern for new engineers to follow.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The templates you use to build cloud infrastructure contain secrets written directly into them, so anyone who can read a template — or its stored deployment history — obtains those secrets. Because templates are often kept in shared repositories, the audience for this exposure is wide. The fix is to remove secrets from templates and reference a secret store or a protected parameter instead. Note that clearing the template is not always sufficient: a secret passed as a plain parameter is recorded in the deployment history, so the history needs checking too. Any secret found should be rotated on the assumption it has been read.

tools: AWS CLI / Azure CLI (for credential validation)
links: CWE-312 (Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information)
AWS CloudFormation documentation: Dynamic references for secrets

items.title: Insecure Auto-Scaling Group Launch Template with Embedded Secrets
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target's auto-scaling group / instance-group launch template or launch configuration (console or CLI). Where testing black-box, access to a launched instance from the same launch template/configuration to inspect its user-data/metadata at boot.
items.whatItIs: A server auto-scaling group's setup script (the code that runs automatically on every new server it launches) has a secret — a database password, an API key — typed directly into it, instead of the server fetching that secret securely from a dedicated secrets service when it boots up.
items.rootCause: This bootstrap script is the standard, simplest way to configure a newly-launched server, and putting the secret directly in it seemed simplest at the time. But this setup script stays readable by any process running on that server for its entire lifetime, not just at startup — and it's also visible to anyone who can view the launch configuration itself.
items.impact: Any process or user on the instance can retrieve the full startup configuration, including the embedded secret, through a simple local metadata query. That includes an attacker who compromised the running application through some unrelated flaw. Separately, anyone with permission to read the launch template at the console or API level sees the same secret without ever touching a running instance.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the target's auto-scaling groups/instance groups and review their launch templates/configurations for user-data/custom-data content.
Search the user-data content for secret-shaped values (passwords, keys, tokens) rather than only environment-agnostic bootstrap logic.

Where a running instance from the group is accessible (with authorization), query the instance metadata service directly to confirm the same secret is retrievable locally by any process on the instance, not just visible via console/API review.
Assess whether the secret is unique per environment/deployment or reused identically across the launch template's full history/multiple environments.
Confirm whether the launch template embeds a secret in its user-data, which is readable by any principal able to describe the template.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes reviewing launch-template configuration and querying instance metadata on an authorized test instance from the target group.
Review the launch template's user-data field for embedded secrets via console/API access.

From a running instance launched by the same template, query the local instance-metadata service to retrieve the user-data content and confirm the embedded secret is present and retrievable from within the instance.
Validate the discovered secret's scope of access using a minimal, read-only check.
Document the exact launch template, the secret found, and both the console/API-level and instance-local-level exposure paths.

examplePayloads.label: Review a launch template's user-data content for embedded secrets
Query the instance metadata service locally for the same user-data content
Validate a discovered credential's scope (read-only check)
Decode the launch template's user-data and inspect it for embedded secrets

variants: Secret embedded via cloud-init/user-data directly versus stored in a launch-template-referenced S3 object that's itself insufficiently access-controlled.
Secret retrievable indefinitely from the instance-metadata service throughout the instance's lifetime, distinct from a one-time-use bootstrap token that's rotated immediately after first use.
A secret injected at scale-out through user-data that is also written to the instance's cloud-init log, persisting on every launched instance's disk.
mitigation: Retrieve secrets at boot time from a dedicated secrets-management service (Secrets Manager, Key Vault) using the instance's own IAM role/managed identity, rather than embedding them in user-data at all.
Where user-data must reference a secret's location, pass only a non-sensitive reference (a secret ARN/name) for the boot script to resolve at runtime, never the secret's plaintext value itself.
Restrict launch-template read permissions to the minimal set of principals who genuinely need visibility into instance bootstrap configuration.

Enforce Instance Metadata Service v2 (IMDSv2) with a hop-limit restriction to reduce (though not eliminate) the risk of user-data retrieval via an unrelated server-side request forgery vulnerability elsewhere in the application.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The templates that define how your systems scale up carry secrets embedded in their start-up instructions, and those instructions are readable by anyone able to inspect the template. Worse, they are also written to each new machine's start-up log as it launches, so the secret is copied onto every machine the scaling creates. The fix is to remove secrets from the start-up instructions and have machines retrieve them at run time from a protected store. Because the secret has likely been written to disk across many machines, rotate it rather than assuming removal from the template is enough.

links: CWE-522 (Insufficiently Protected Credentials)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (IMDSv2 enforcement)

items.title: Insecure Cross-Account Role Trust Policy
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's IAM cross-account role trust policies. Access to a test principal in the trusted external account (or the tester's own authorized cross-account test setup) to attempt an actual role assumption.
items.whatItIs: A cloud access role meant for an outside company — a common pattern for vendor access or cross-account automation — is configured too loosely. It may trust that entire external account rather than one specific role or user within it. It may be missing the extra verification value recommended for this kind of access. Or it may grant more permissions once assumed than the relationship actually requires.
items.rootCause: This kind of cross-account trust is usually set up as broadly as needed to just get it working ("anyone in vendor account X can use this role"), because narrowing it down further takes more coordination with the outside party. The permissions granted once someone assumes that role are often just as loosely set, for the same reason — convenience over precision.
items.impact: If the trusted external account is ever compromised, the attacker inherits the ability to assume the role and use whatever it grants. This is a real and documented risk for third-party vendor accounts in particular, because they sit outside the organisation's own security control. The result is a direct route into the organisation's cloud environment that sidesteps every control applied to its own directly-managed accounts.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all IAM roles in the account with a trust policy referencing an external account principal, and review each trust policy's exact condition (account-wide trust vs. a specific role/user, presence/absence of an External ID condition).
For each cross-account role found, review its attached permission policy for scope — is it narrowly tailored to the specific cross-account use case, or does it grant broad, unrelated permissions.

Where feasible and authorized, verify with the client which external accounts are legitimately expected to hold this trust relationship, and confirm the external account ID in the trust policy actually matches a currently-valid, expected partner.

Check whether an External ID condition is present for any third-party vendor trust relationship specifically, since its absence is a well-documented confused-deputy risk pattern for this exact scenario.
Establish how narrowly the cross-account trust is conditioned, since a trust lacking an external-id or specific-principal condition can be assumed by an unintended account.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes testing cross-account role assumption from an authorized test principal in the trusted external account (or the tester's own equivalent authorized setup).
Attempt to assume the target role from the test principal, confirming the trust policy's condition is as broad as identified during discovery.
Once assumed, enumerate the permissions the role grants and attempt a benign, read-only action to confirm practical access, without performing any destructive or data-exfiltrating action.

Where an External ID is absent, and where authorized to demonstrate the confused-deputy risk specifically, illustrate how a different customer/tenant of the same external vendor (in a genuine multi-tenant SaaS cross-account scenario) could potentially assume the same role if the vendor's own tenant-isolation controls were ever insufficient.
Document the exact trust-policy condition, the role's granted permissions, and the specific gap (account-wide trust, missing External ID, excessive permissions) found.

examplePayloads.label: Review a role's cross-account trust policy
Attempt role assumption from the trusted external test account
Enumerate the assumed role's effective permissions
Inspect the cross-account role's trust policy for a missing external-id condition

variants: Trust policy scoped to a specific role/user in the external account but still missing an External ID condition, leaving a residual confused-deputy risk in specific multi-tenant vendor scenarios.

Trust policy appropriately narrow, but the role's attached permission policy is far broader than the cross-account use case requires, providing excessive impact even if the trust boundary itself is sound.
A trust correctly conditioned on a partner account that has itself been compromised, extending the exposure through the trusted third party rather than around it.
mitigation: Scope cross-account trust policies to the specific, minimal external role/user needed, avoiding account-wide trust conditions.

Include an External ID condition (a unique, hard-to-guess value shared out-of-band with the external party) for any third-party vendor cross-account trust relationship, per the cloud provider's own confused-deputy mitigation guidance.
Apply least privilege to the role's attached permission policy, scoping it to only the specific actions/resources the cross-account use case genuinely requires.
Periodically re-verify that every external account referenced in a trust policy remains a current, legitimate partner, removing stale trust relationships from completed engagements/migrations.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A trust relationship that lets another cloud account act within yours is configured too loosely, so an account you did not intend could assume it and gain the access it grants. Cross-account trust is a normal and useful mechanism, but it needs a specific condition — a shared secret identifier, a named principal — to ensure only the intended partner can use it, and that condition is missing or too broad here. The fix is to tighten the trust so it admits only the specific account it was built for. Bear in mind that even a correctly scoped trust extends your exposure to that partner's own security, which is worth weighing.

links: CWE-441 (Unintended Proxy or Intermediary - Confused Deputy)
AWS documentation: The confused deputy problem

items.title: Insecure Cross-Region Replication Exposing Data Residency
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's data-replication configuration (cross-region replication rules on storage buckets/databases) and, where relevant, the organization's data-residency/compliance requirements documentation to assess against.
items.whatItIs: A cloud storage bucket or database automatically copies its data to a geographic region the company's data-residency rules, or a law such as GDPR, do not allow. The replication is usually set up for a legitimate reason: disaster recovery, or faster access for users in that region. What was never checked is whether that destination is actually permitted for this specific data.
items.rootCause: Cross-region replication gets configured based on purely technical reasons — where users are, how to survive an outage — without a matching compliance review to confirm the destination region is actually permitted for that category of data. Data residency ends up as an afterthought to what was primarily a technical decision.
items.impact: Regulated or contractually restricted data ends up stored somewhere the organisation is not permitted to store it. That might be personal data under GDPR, data covered by a national residency law, or data governed by a residency clause in a customer contract. The exposure is regulatory and contractual, and it exists whether or not anyone unauthorised ever actually reads the replicated copy.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all cross-region replication configurations across the target's storage buckets and databases, noting source and destination regions for each.

Cross-reference each destination region against the organization's documented data-residency requirements and any customer-contract or regulatory obligations covering the specific data category being replicated.

For any replication configuration found to violate a residency requirement, confirm what data category is actually flowing through it (via bucket/database naming, tags, or a sample content review) rather than assuming based on the resource name alone.
Check whether the replication was a deliberate, reviewed architectural decision (with a documented compliance exception) versus an unreviewed default applied for purely technical reasons.
Establish which regions the replication targets, since replication into a region outside the agreed data-residency boundary is itself the finding.
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through configuration and compliance-requirement review rather than actively exploited by the tester, since the "impact" is a compliance/regulatory exposure rather than a directly attacker-exploitable technical vulnerability.
Confirm scope authorizes reviewing replication configuration and, where necessary, a sample of the actual replicated data to confirm its category.
Document each replication configuration found to violate a residency requirement, the specific regulation/contract clause implicated, and the data category confirmed present in the replicated copy.

Present findings in terms the client's compliance/legal function can act on directly (which regulation, which specific data, which region), since remediation ownership for this finding often sits outside the purely technical security team.
Confirm the replicated copy in the unintended region is readable and un-deleted, establishing that the residency breach is live rather than historical.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate a bucket's cross-region replication configuration
Enumerate a database's cross-region read-replica/replication configuration
Sample the replicated destination bucket/database to confirm data category present
List the bucket's replication rules and their destination regions

variants: Replication configured for disaster-recovery purposes across regions that individually satisfy residency requirements when considered alone, but whose combination inadvertently transits through or is processed by an intermediate, non-compliant region during the replication process itself.
Data-residency violation introduced not via bucket/database replication directly, but via a CDN edge-caching configuration that caches content in edge locations outside the required jurisdiction.
Replication that respects the residency boundary for the primary data but not for its access logs, which leak the same records into a non-compliant region.
mitigation: Establish a mandatory data-residency/compliance review step as part of any cross-region replication design, before enabling the configuration, not after.

Tag data resources with their applicable residency/compliance classification, and use policy-as-code tooling to automatically flag or block replication configurations that would move a tagged resource outside its permitted region set.

Where disaster-recovery diversity is needed for compliance-restricted data, select a DR region that itself satisfies the same residency requirement rather than defaulting to the provider's standard DR-region recommendation.

Periodically audit all replication configurations against current residency/compliance requirements, since regulations and contractual obligations can change independently of the technical configuration.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your data is being copied to another region in a way that may place it outside the geographic boundary your obligations require it to stay within. This is less a break-in than a compliance and data-residency exposure: the copy is legitimate infrastructure, but its destination is wrong. The fix is to confirm which regions replication targets and to constrain it to those permitted, then verify the copy already made in the unintended region is removed. Check the access logs too, since a common oversight is replicating the primary data compliantly while its logs — carrying the same records — leak into a non-compliant region.

items.title: Insecure Lambda/Function Layer Dependency Confusion
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target serverless function's/deployment package's dependency manifest (package.json, requirements.txt, or an equivalent lock file). Ability to publish a test package to the relevant public package registry (npm, PyPI) under a name matching an internal-only package, with authorization and using an unmistakably-labeled proof-of-concept package.
items.whatItIs: A cloud function's build process pulls in a required software package by name from a public registry (like npm or PyPI), without any guarantee that an internal, privately-named package will always be chosen over a public package that happens to share the same name. An attacker can publish a malicious package under that same name publicly, and it gets installed instead of — or alongside — the real internal one, running their code inside the build or runtime.
items.rootCause: The internal package's name was never registered as protected/private on the registry, and the build tool checks the public registry either exclusively or in a way that can be tricked (for example, a higher version number on the attacker's public package winning by default). The whole problem comes from trusting a package name to uniquely and safely identify the right package — which isn't actually true once both a private and public package can share that name.
items.impact: A malicious package published under a matching name, with a version that wins resolution, gets installed and its code runs. Where that happens decides the damage. If it runs during the build, the attacker gets code execution in the CI/CD environment and whatever secrets that environment holds. If it runs at function runtime, they get execution inside the deployed function instead.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the target's internal/private package names referenced in dependency manifests (via any available internal documentation, package.json/requirements.txt files, or internal package registry listings, with appropriate authorization).

For each internal package name identified, check the public registry (npmjs.com, pypi.org) to determine whether a package with that exact name already exists there — if the name is genuinely unclaimed on the public registry, dependency confusion is likely feasible.

Review the target's build/CI configuration for how it resolves package sources — does it correctly prioritize an internal/private registry via an explicit scope or registry-priority configuration, or does it fall through to the public registry by default for any unscoped package name.

Assess the build pipeline's resolution algorithm (does it always pick the highest semantic version across all configured sources, which is the classic dependency-confusion-enabling default) to confirm the vulnerability is genuinely exploitable rather than merely theoretically possible.
Confirm whether the function resolves a dependency from a public source that an attacker could pre-register under the same name.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes publishing a clearly-labeled, benign proof-of-concept package to the public registry under the target's internal package name — this step affects a shared public resource and needs unambiguous authorization and a clear teardown plan.

Publish a proof-of-concept package with a version number designed to win typical dependency-resolution precedence (a high semantic version) and a payload limited to a benign, easily-identifiable side effect (e.g. writing a uniquely-named marker file or making a single outbound callback to a controlled, logged endpoint) — never a destructive or data-exfiltrating payload.

Trigger (or wait for) the target's next build/deployment cycle and monitor the controlled callback endpoint or check build logs (where accessible with authorization) for evidence the proof-of-concept package was resolved and executed.

Immediately unpublish/remove the proof-of-concept package from the public registry once the finding is confirmed, and document the exact package name, registry, and resolution-precedence behavior observed.
Confirm the resolver prefers the public source over the private one for the disputed name, establishing the confusion is exploitable rather than theoretical.

examplePayloads.label: Check whether an internal package name is unclaimed on the public npm registry
examplePayloads.command: npm view <internal-package-name>  # a 404/not-found response indicates the name is available for a dependency-confusion attempt

examplePayloads.label: Publish a benign, clearly-labeled proof-of-concept package (authorized test only)
examplePayloads.command: npm publish  # package.json name matches the target internal package, version set higher than the internal one, with only a benign postinstall script making a single callback to a controlled test endpoint

examplePayloads.label: Check the build pipeline's registry configuration for scoping/priority
examplePayloads.command: cat .npmrc  # look for a missing or incorrect @internal-scope:registry= directive

examplePayloads.label: Inspect the function's declared dependencies for internally-named packages resolvable publicly

variants: Dependency confusion via a build-time-only dependency (a dev/test-only package) that executes during CI rather than in the deployed runtime, still yielding CI-environment code execution and secret access.
Dependency confusion via a transitive dependency (an internal package's own internal sub-dependency) rather than a top-level, directly-referenced package name.
Confusion at the shared-layer level rather than the package level, where a layer name resolvable by a broader principal is substituted.
mitigation: Reserve/claim the organization's internal package names on the relevant public registries (even as empty placeholder packages) to prevent an attacker from squatting on them.

Use registry scoping (npm's `@scope` mechanism, or an equivalent private-registry-only configuration) so internal package names are unambiguously namespaced and cannot be shadowed by an identically-named public package.
Configure the build pipeline to resolve internal packages exclusively from the internal/private registry, with no fallback to the public registry for those specific package names.

Pin exact dependency versions (rather than a version range) in lock files, and verify package integrity via lock-file hashes, to reduce the window for a resolution-precedence attack even where scoping isn't fully in place.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your cloud functions pull in external code components by name, and for some internally-named components an attacker could publish a public component of the same name that your systems would fetch and run instead of yours. This lets attacker code execute inside your environment through the supply chain rather than a direct attack. The fix is to ensure internal components are always resolved from your private source and can never be satisfied by a public one of the same name. This is a subtle but well-documented attack, and it is worth confirming explicitly because the failure runs your build against a stranger's code.

items.title: Insecure Multi-Tenant Cloud Isolation (Shared Compute Escape)
items.prerequisites: An authorized tenant/account within the target's shared multi-tenant compute environment (a shared Kubernetes cluster, a shared serverless platform, or a shared VM-hosting environment where the organization is itself a tenant of a third-party provider). Standard container/process-inspection tooling reachable from within the tenant's own workload.
items.whatItIs: Multiple customers share the same underlying cloud infrastructure — the same cluster, the same virtualization host — with isolation between them enforced only by the platform's software boundary (containers, namespaces, or a hypervisor). A gap in that boundary — an overly loose shared setting, a hypervisor bug, or a misconfigured permission rule — can let one customer's workload access or interfere with another's, even though they're not supposed to be able to see each other at all.
items.rootCause: Isolation between tenants depends entirely on that boundary mechanism working correctly — container isolation, hypervisor-level virtualization, or specific access-control rules in something like Kubernetes. Any gap in any layer of that boundary — a missing rule restricting cross-tenant traffic, a permission scoped too broadly, or an unpatched low-level platform bug — directly breaks the isolation the whole shared-infrastructure model depends on.
items.impact: A malicious or compromised tenant sharing the same infrastructure can reach another tenant's data, workloads or credentials. They never have to get past that tenant's own external security, because the failure happens underneath it, at the shared infrastructure layer. This is especially serious for any customer treating the platform's isolation as their primary security boundary.
stepsToIdentify: From within the organization's own tenant/namespace on the shared platform, enumerate what network paths, shared kernel resources, or platform APIs are reachable, and test whether any of them expose cross-tenant scope beyond the organization's own workloads.

For a Kubernetes-based shared cluster specifically, review NetworkPolicy configuration for whether cross-namespace traffic is genuinely restricted, and review RBAC role bindings for whether any role/service-account inadvertently has visibility across tenant namespace boundaries.

Check the platform's own security-advisory history for any known hypervisor/container-runtime escape vulnerability that might affect the specific version in use, especially if a patch has been announced but not yet confirmed applied.

Where the concern is a shared serverless platform, assess whether concurrent function executions from different tenants can ever share the same underlying execution container/warm-start environment in a way that leaks state between invocations.
Establish whether tenant isolation relies on shared compute with logical separation rather than dedicated resources, since the former carries side-channel and escape exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes attempting cross-tenant boundary testing on the shared platform — this is unusually sensitive given the platform is often operated by a third party, so authorization should ideally involve or at minimum be transparent to the platform provider, not just the immediate client.

From the organization's own authorized tenant, attempt to reach network resources, shared kernel interfaces, or platform APIs that should be scoped to other tenants, using only non-destructive, read-only probes.

Where a specific, known escape/isolation-bypass vulnerability applies to the platform's current version, attempt a controlled, minimally-invasive proof-of-concept limited strictly to the organization's own tenant boundary (never actually crossing into another real customer's tenant, given the shared, live nature of the environment).

Document any confirmed isolation gap precisely, distinguishing between a theoretical/patched vulnerability (informational) and a practically demonstrated cross-tenant reachability issue (a genuine, high-severity finding).

Given the inherently sensitive and third-party nature of this finding, escalate promptly to both the client and, where appropriate, the platform provider rather than treating it as a standard report-and-wait finding.

examplePayloads.label: Review NetworkPolicy configuration for cross-namespace traffic restriction (Kubernetes)
Review RBAC role bindings for cross-namespace scope
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.namespace != .metadata.namespace)'

examplePayloads.label: From within the tenant's own pod, test reachability to a network range that should belong to another tenant's namespace only
Confirm whether workloads from different tenants share the same underlying nodes

variants: Isolation gap at the Kubernetes namespace/RBAC configuration layer (a fixable, in-organization-control misconfiguration) versus a hypervisor/container-runtime-level escape vulnerability (a platform-provider responsibility to patch).
Serverless-platform warm-start container reuse across different tenants' invocations leaking residual memory/state, distinct from a network-level cross-tenant reachability issue.
Isolation enforced at the compute layer but not at the shared-cache or message-bus layer, where one tenant's data transits infrastructure another tenant can reach.
mitigation: Apply strict Kubernetes NetworkPolicies denying all cross-namespace traffic by default, with narrow, explicit allow-rules only where genuinely required.
Scope RBAC roles and service accounts strictly to their own namespace, auditing for any binding that inadvertently grants cross-namespace visibility.

Where the isolation gap stems from a platform-level (hypervisor/runtime) vulnerability, escalate to the platform provider for patching and consider dedicated (non-shared) infrastructure for the most sensitive workloads in the interim.

For workloads with the highest sensitivity/compliance requirements, evaluate whether a shared multi-tenant platform is the appropriate hosting model at all, versus dedicated, single-tenant infrastructure.
items.mitigationClientFacing: In your multi-tenant setup, the separation between one customer's workloads and another's relies on shared infrastructure with logical boundaries rather than genuinely separate resources. That leaves room for one tenant's data to be reached by another through a weakness in the shared layer — a side effect, a cache, a message channel that the compute-level isolation does not cover. The fix is to strengthen isolation at every shared layer, not only compute, and where the data is sensitive enough, to move to dedicated resources per tenant. This matters most where the tenants are mutually untrusted, since the boundary is what your customers are relying on.
