items.title: Insecure Secrets Manager Access Policy (Overly Broad)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's secrets-management service configuration (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) and its associated access policies. A test IAM principal with limited, unrelated permissions to confirm whether it can unexpectedly reach secrets it shouldn't.
items.whatItIs: The permissions on a secrets-management service grant read access more broadly than needed. Typically that is a blanket rule covering every secret in the account, rather than only the ones a given team requires. The practical result is that one team can read another team's secrets stored in the same shared service.
items.rootCause: These permissions are often set up at the broadest, simplest level for convenience — granting access to 'all secrets' instead of listing out exactly which ones are needed — because setting up narrower, per-secret rules takes more upfront work and ongoing maintenance as new secrets get added. This convenience directly undoes the whole point of using a secrets service in the first place: giving each team access to only what it actually needs.
items.impact: Any account holding the over-broad policy can read every secret it covers. That includes an account compromised through a completely unrelated flaw in an application that only ever needed one specific secret. What should have been a contained, single-application credential compromise becomes an organisation-wide secrets exposure.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the access policies attached to the target's secrets-management service and identify any using a wildcard resource scope or an overly broad principal/role assignment.
For each broadly-scoped policy, map which principals/roles it applies to and what secrets each of those principals actually needs, to quantify the gap between granted and required access.

With authorization, test a specific, narrowly-purposed test principal's actual reach by attempting to retrieve a secret unrelated to its intended function, confirming whether the broad policy allows this in practice, not just in the written policy configuration.
Check for a secrets-tagging/labeling scheme that could support a more granular policy design, to assess remediation feasibility alongside the finding itself.
Confirm how broadly the secret's access policy grants retrieval, since a wildcard principal or resource turns one secret store into an open one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes testing actual secret-retrieval reach using a designated, narrowly-purposed test IAM principal.
Using the test principal's credentials, attempt to list and retrieve secrets outside its intended, documented functional scope.

Where retrieval succeeds, document exactly which unrelated secrets were reachable and validate (with a minimal, read-only check) that at least one represents a genuine, currently-live credential rather than a stale/placeholder value.
Map the full population of principals subject to the same overly-broad policy to characterize the true scope of the exposure, not just the single test principal used for the demonstration.
Document the exact policy configuration responsible and recommend the specific, narrower scope that would satisfy the legitimate functional need.

examplePayloads.label: Review a secrets-management resource policy for overly broad scope
Attempt retrieval of an unrelated secret using a narrowly-purposed test principal
Enumerate all secrets a given role can access
Inspect the secret's resource policy for overly broad principals

variants: Overly broad access granted at the secrets-management-service level (a wildcard resource ARN) versus overly broad access granted via a separately overly-permissive IAM policy attached to the consuming role, even where the secrets-service-level policy itself is properly scoped.
Legacy access grant left in place from an earlier, less mature stage of the secrets-management rollout, before per-application scoping practices were established.
A policy scoped correctly on the secret but undermined by a broad decrypt permission on the key that protects it, which grants indirect access.
mitigation: Scope every secrets-management access policy to the specific, named secret(s) a given principal genuinely needs, avoiding wildcard resource scopes entirely.

Adopt a consistent secrets-naming/tagging convention (by application/team) that supports attribute-based access policies scaling cleanly as new secrets are added, rather than requiring a policy rewrite for every new secret.
Periodically audit secrets-management access policies against actual usage patterns (via access logs) to identify and narrow any grant that's broader than what's actually being used.

Apply the same least-privilege review rigor to secrets-management policies as to any other IAM policy, since a secrets-management misconfiguration undermines the security benefit of centralizing secrets in the first place.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The policy governing who can read your stored secrets grants access too broadly, so more principals than intended can retrieve them. A secret store is only as good as the policy protecting it, and a broad grant turns a vault into an open shelf. The fix is to scope each secret's access to the specific principals that genuinely need it. Check the key that encrypts the secrets as well: a tightly-scoped secret protected by a broadly-shared encryption key is still reachable, because permission to decrypt the key grants indirect access to what it protects.

items.title: Insecure Serverless Function Resource Abuse (Denial of Wallet)
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target serverless function's public-facing invocation endpoint (an API Gateway URL or a direct function URL). A load-generation tool capable of sustained, high-volume invocation (a scripted loop, or a load-testing tool like hey/vegeta).
items.whatItIs: A serverless function (billed based on how often it runs and how much compute it uses) can be triggered publicly with no limit on how many times, allowing an attacker to trigger it an enormous number of times. This doesn't necessarily take the service down — the cloud might just auto-scale to handle the load — but it can drive the company's cloud bill to an unsustainable level, purely from requests that look completely legitimate.
items.rootCause: Serverless platforms are specifically built to automatically scale up to handle demand, which is great for real traffic spikes but becomes a liability with no volume-based limit or cost cap layered on top. Without a hard ceiling on how many times something can be triggered, the usual 'the service goes down' failure mode gets replaced with a purely financial one — the service stays fully available, but the bill keeps climbing.
items.impact: Sustained abuse can produce a bill many times the function's normal running cost in a short window. The awkward part is that each individual invocation may look entirely legitimate — no malformed input, no attack signatures. Monitoring tuned to error rates or malicious payloads will not flag any of it, so the first real signal is often the cost itself, by which point the spend is already significant.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all publicly-invokable serverless functions/API Gateway endpoints in the target environment and review each for configured rate limiting, invocation quotas, or cost-based alerting.

Check whether the function's billing model (per-invocation, per-GB-second of compute) and its configured maximum concurrency/timeout create a realistic worst-case cost ceiling, or whether that ceiling is effectively unbounded given current configuration.

Review whether a budget alert or cost-anomaly-detection mechanism is in place specifically covering this function/API, independent of the general account-wide cost-monitoring already assessed in the related cryptomining-cost-anomaly finding.

Assess whether the function performs any particularly expensive operation per invocation (a large data transformation, an external paid-API call) that would amplify the per-invocation cost impact of a denial-of-wallet attempt.
Establish whether the function has a concurrency ceiling, since without one a single caller can drive unbounded parallel execution and cost.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes a bounded, cost-aware load-testing demonstration against the target function, and agree an explicit invocation-volume/cost ceiling with the client before starting, given the direct financial risk of this specific test.

Establish the function's baseline per-invocation cost (from its billing configuration and typical execution duration) to calculate a safe, bounded test volume that demonstrates the vulnerability without incurring a materially significant bill.

Generate a sustained, bounded burst of invocations using a load-testing tool and confirm whether the platform accepts and processes all of them without any rate-limiting response (429) or invocation-quota rejection.

Extrapolate the demonstrated per-invocation cost to a realistic sustained-attack scenario (e.g. projected cost over 24 hours at the demonstrated rate) as the primary business-impact evidence, rather than running the actual attack to that scale.
Document the absence of any rate limit/quota/circuit-breaker and the extrapolated cost-impact projection for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Establish baseline single-invocation cost and duration
Bounded load-test burst to confirm absence of rate limiting (agree volume ceiling with client first)
Check for configured usage plans/throttling on the API Gateway front-end
Confirm whether a concurrency limit is configured on the function

variants: Denial-of-wallet targeting a function that itself calls a paid third-party API per invocation, multiplying the cost-per-invocation impact well beyond the cloud platform's own compute billing alone.
Denial-of-wallet via an authenticated but insufficiently rate-limited endpoint, exploitable by any registered user rather than requiring a fully public/unauthenticated endpoint.
Abuse of a function triggered by an event source rather than a direct call, where flooding the source multiplies invocations indirectly.
mitigation: Configure an API Gateway usage plan with a defined rate limit and burst quota for every publicly-invokable function endpoint, rejecting excess invocations with a 429 rather than processing them.
Set a hard concurrency limit on the function itself as a platform-level circuit-breaker, bounding the worst-case cost regardless of invocation volume.

Configure cost-anomaly alerting and, where the platform supports it, an automated response (throttling or temporary disablement) tied specifically to this function's spend, not just account-wide billing review.
For functions that call paid third-party APIs per invocation, apply an additional, tighter internal rate limit reflecting that amplified per-invocation cost specifically.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your serverless functions have no ceiling on how much they will run in response to demand, so an attacker can trigger them relentlessly to run up costs or exhaust capacity — the cloud equivalent of leaving a tap that bills you per drop with no way to shut it off. The fix is to set a sensible concurrency limit on each function so that abuse is capped rather than unbounded, and to protect the event sources that trigger functions indirectly. This is both an availability and a cost control, and it is inexpensive to apply relative to the size of bill it prevents.

items.title: Insecure Third-Party Cloud Marketplace AMI with Backdoor
items.prerequisites: Access to the specific third-party cloud-marketplace AMI/machine image under test, deployed to an isolated, disposable test instance/account. Standard forensic/inspection tooling (file-integrity checking, network-connection monitoring, decompilation tools) to analyze the image's actual runtime behavior.
items.whatItIs: A virtual machine image obtained from a cloud marketplace — rather than built by the company or the cloud provider — has malicious functionality deliberately built in by whoever published it. That might be a hidden backdoor account, a covert connection back to the attacker, or code that quietly steals data and credentials from any server launched using the image.
items.rootCause: Cloud marketplaces let outside publishers list images with fairly limited checking of what's actually inside — the platform usually verifies who the publisher is and basic policy compliance, not a deep security audit of every file in the image. So launching a server from a marketplace image means implicitly trusting that specific publisher's software, with no independent check of your own.
items.impact: An instance launched from a backdoored image is compromised the moment it boots, potentially before the organisation's own security tooling is even installed on it. The backdoor runs with whatever access that instance has, which can include the cloud role attached to it. The attacker's foothold therefore predates every control the organisation would normally apply.
stepsToIdentify: Review the marketplace listing's publisher reputation, review history, and update cadence — an unmaintained image from an obscure, unverified publisher warrants more scrutiny than one from a well-established, verified vendor.

Launch the image to an isolated, disposable test instance/account with no production data or credentials attached, and monitor its outbound network connections immediately upon boot, before any organization-specific configuration is applied.
Inspect the image's installed software, running processes, and scheduled tasks/cron jobs for anything unexpected relative to the image's advertised purpose.
Check for hardcoded credentials, unexpected listening services, or SSH authorized_keys entries pre-populated with a key the organization didn't provision.
Establish the provenance of the marketplace image, since a community image lacks the vendor accountability of an official one and may carry planted content.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes launching and forensically inspecting the target marketplace image in an isolated test environment.
Launch the image to a disposable test instance with no sensitive data or production IAM role attached, and monitor its behavior from the very first boot.
Capture all outbound network connections during boot and normal idle operation, flagging any callback to an unexpected, non-vendor-documented destination.
Inspect installed software and configuration for backdoor indicators (unexpected user accounts, pre-populated SSH keys, unexplained scheduled tasks).

Where a backdoor indicator is confirmed, document it precisely (the specific file/account/connection) and immediately terminate the test instance, recommending the client cease using the image and audit any production instance already launched from it.

examplePayloads.label: Monitor outbound connections from a freshly-launched test instance
Check for unexpected pre-populated SSH authorized keys
Enumerate scheduled tasks/cron jobs for unexpected entries
Check for unexpected listening services

variants: Backdoor present in the image's base OS layer versus embedded specifically in a bundled application/agent the marketplace listing advertises as its main value proposition.

Malicious behavior triggered only under specific conditions (a time-delayed logic bomb, a beacon that only activates once real production traffic/data is detected) rather than being immediately observable at first boot.
A backdoor present not in the base image but in a bundled initialisation script that runs on first boot, evading a scan of the image filesystem at rest.
mitigation: Prefer building custom images from a trusted, minimal base (the cloud provider's own official base images) over third-party marketplace images wherever the required software can reasonably be installed and configured directly.

Where a marketplace image must be used, launch it first to an isolated test environment for a forensic review (as described above) before any production deployment, and repeat this review for any image update.

Restrict the IAM role/permissions attached to any instance launched from an unverified third-party image to the absolute minimum, limiting the blast radius if the image is later found to be compromised.

Monitor production instances launched from marketplace images with the same (or greater) scrutiny as internet-facing, externally-developed software, including outbound-connection monitoring and file-integrity checking.
items.mitigationClientFacing: One of your machines was launched from a shared marketplace image of uncertain origin, and such community images can contain planted backdoors that give their author access to every machine built from them. Unlike an official vendor image, a community one carries no accountability for what is inside it. The fix is to build from trusted, official or self-maintained images whose contents you can verify, and to treat any machine already launched from an untrusted image as potentially compromised. Note that a backdoor can hide in a start-up script that runs on first boot rather than in the image's files, so a static scan is not sufficient assurance.

items.title: Missing Cloud WAF on Public-Facing Load Balancer
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target's public-facing cloud load balancer/CDN endpoint. Standard web-application-attack payloads (a basic SQL injection probe, an XSS probe) for a benign, non-destructive test of whether a WAF layer intercepts them, plus the ability to review the load balancer/CDN configuration directly if white-box access is available.
items.whatItIs: A public-facing load balancer or CDN serving the company's website has no Web Application Firewall attached. Alternatively it has one, but set only to log suspicious traffic rather than block it. Either way the application's own code is the only real defence against common attacks such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting, with nothing filtering traffic before it arrives.
items.rootCause: Setting up a WAF is a separate step beyond just standing up a load balancer or CDN, and it's often postponed or left in 'monitor only' mode during initial rollout to avoid accidentally blocking real traffic — without a later step to switch it into actual blocking mode once it's been tuned. The extra protective layer ends up either missing entirely, or present but not actually doing anything.
items.impact: The application is directly exposed to high-volume automated attack traffic — injection probes, known-bad bot scanning, credential-stuffing tools — with nothing filtering it first. Every one of those patterns reaches the application's own code. Defence rests entirely on that application's input validation and business logic, against exactly the class of attack a firewall layer is designed to absorb cheaply before it ever arrives.
stepsToIdentify: Check the target load balancer/CDN distribution's configuration (via console/CLI, with authorization) for an attached WAF web ACL, and if present, its rule action (block vs. count-only).

Send a benign, clearly-non-destructive attack-pattern probe (a basic SQLi/XSS test string in a request parameter, not a functional exploit) and observe whether the request is blocked at the edge (a WAF-generated 403) or reaches the application layer for processing.
Where a WAF is present but in count-only mode, review its logging/monitoring dashboard (if accessible) to confirm it is indeed only logging matches rather than blocking them.

Assess whether any managed rule set (an OWASP Core Rule Set equivalent, a cloud-provider-managed rule group) is enabled at all, versus only a custom, narrowly-scoped rule set that wouldn't catch the broader class of common attacks.
Confirm whether the protective layer is genuinely absent or present in detection-only mode, since a monitoring-only deployment blocks nothing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes sending benign attack-pattern probe traffic against the target public-facing endpoint to test WAF presence/behavior.

Send a representative set of common attack-pattern probes (non-functional, clearly-benign versions — e.g. a SQLi test string that would trigger detection signatures without actually being a working injection against the specific application) and observe the response.

Confirm whether each probe reached the application (a normal application-generated response, possibly an application-level error) versus being intercepted at the edge (a WAF-generated block page/403).
Where a WAF is present but not blocking, document this distinctly from a complete WAF absence, since remediation (a mode change) differs from initial deployment.
Document which specific attack-pattern categories were and weren't intercepted, to give the client a concrete picture of current coverage gaps.

examplePayloads.label: Check for an attached WAF web ACL on the target distribution
Send a benign SQLi-pattern probe to test WAF interception
Send an encoded XSS signature to test whether the WAF intercepts it
Confirm whether a protective layer is associated with the load balancer at all

variants: WAF present and actively blocking for one distribution/endpoint (e.g. the primary marketing site) but absent or in count-only mode for a separate, equally public-facing API endpoint or secondary application.
WAF present with a managed rule set enabled but a custom exclusion rule inadvertently created during tuning that whitelists a broader-than-intended request pattern.
Protection attached to the primary endpoint but absent from an alternate origin or direct backend address, which becomes the unprotected path around it.
mitigation: Deploy a WAF (the cloud provider's native offering or a third-party equivalent) in front of every public-facing load balancer/CDN distribution, with a recognized managed rule set (an OWASP Core Rule Set equivalent) enabled as a baseline.
Transition any WAF currently running in count/log-only mode to active blocking mode once an appropriate tuning period has confirmed an acceptably low false-positive rate against legitimate traffic.

Periodically re-test WAF effectiveness with benign attack-pattern probes (as used in this identification process) as a standing check, since rule-set updates or configuration changes can silently regress coverage.
Treat the WAF as a compensating, defense-in-depth control rather than a substitute for proper input validation and secure coding practice within the application itself.
items.mitigationClientFacing: One of your internet-facing services has no protective filtering layer in front of it, so common automated attacks reach the application directly rather than being screened out first. A filtering layer is not a substitute for a secure application, but it removes a large volume of routine attack traffic and buys time to patch when a new weakness emerges. The fix is to place one in front of the exposed service and, importantly, to run it in blocking rather than monitoring-only mode — a layer that watches but does not block provides visibility without protection. Confirm it also covers any alternate address that reaches the same backend.

items.title: Overly Permissive IAM Policy (Wildcard Actions/Resources)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's IAM policies (managed and inline) attached to users, groups, and roles. AWS CLI or the equivalent for the cloud provider in use, configured with read-only IAM inspection permissions.
items.whatItIs: A cloud permissions policy grants access using a wildcard — meaning 'any action' or 'any resource' — instead of listing out the specific things a person or system actually needs to do. This usually happens for convenience during initial setup ('just make it work') and is never narrowed down later once it becomes clear what the minimum needed permissions actually are.
items.rootCause: Writing a tightly-scoped permissions policy requires knowing in advance (or figuring out through careful review) the complete, specific list of actions and resources something needs — which takes real effort. It's much easier to just grant a broad wildcard that's guaranteed to work for anything now or later. That convenience-over-precision tradeoff is, by a wide margin, the single most common reason cloud permissions end up too broad.
items.impact: An account holding a wildcard policy can do far more than its actual job requires. If its credentials are ever compromised — through a leaked access key, an exploited application flaw, or anything else unrelated to permissions themselves — the result is full or near-full control of the cloud account. A properly scoped policy would have confined the same compromise to a narrow, survivable blast radius.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all IAM policies (managed and inline) across users, groups, and roles in the account, flagging any with an `"Action": "*"`, broad service-wildcard action, or `"Resource": "*"` element.

For each flagged policy, use the cloud provider's access-analyzer/last-accessed-services tooling to determine what the attached principal has actually used over a representative historical period, quantifying the gap between granted and actually-used permissions.

Prioritize findings by the principal's actual reach — a wildcard policy on a rarely-used, low-privilege test account is lower severity than the same wildcard on a principal with broad network/data access or one used by an internet-facing service.

Check whether any policy combines a wildcard action with an otherwise-narrow resource scope (or vice versa), since a wildcard on only one dimension is still a significant, if smaller, over-permissioning issue relative to a policy wildcarded on both dimensions simultaneously.
Establish which wildcard actions the policy grants and on which resources, since a wildcard on both is effectively administrative regardless of the role's name.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes IAM policy review and, where applicable, an authorized demonstration using a principal holding one of the identified wildcard policies.
Using the flagged principal's credentials (with authorization), attempt a range of actions well outside its documented, intended function to confirm the wildcard grant permits them in practice.

Where feasible, demonstrate a concrete escalation path enabled by the wildcard — for example, a principal with `iam:*` wildcarded can typically create or modify its own or another principal's policy to grant itself full administrative access, which is worth demonstrating explicitly as the clearest illustration of the risk.
Document each wildcard policy found, the specific unused-but-granted actions confirmed via testing, and, where demonstrated, the concrete escalation path it enables.
Confirm at least one granted wildcard permission is usable to reach a resource beyond the role's intended scope, establishing real over-privilege rather than nominal breadth.

examplePayloads.label: Search all IAM policies for wildcard action/resource elements
examplePayloads.command: aws iam list-policies --scope Local --query 'Policies[].Arn' | xargs -I{} aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn {} --version-id $(aws iam get-policy --policy-arn {} --query 'Policy.DefaultVersionId' --output text)

examplePayloads.label: Check what a flagged principal has actually used recently (IAM Access Analyzer)
Demonstrate a self-escalation path via an iam:* wildcarded principal (authorized test only)
Enumerate the policy's granted actions and flag wildcards

variants: Wildcard action combined with a narrow, specific resource ARN (lower severity — the blast radius is bounded to that resource, but the principal can still perform any action against it).
Wildcard resource combined with a narrow, specific action (e.g. `s3:GetObject` on `Resource: *`) — bounded to one action type, but across every resource of that type in the account.
Over-privilege assembled across several narrowly-scoped policies that combine to an administrative effect, which review of any single policy misses.
mitigation: Replace every wildcard-action/resource policy with a scoped policy enumerating the specific actions and resource ARNs the principal's actual, documented function requires.

Use the cloud provider's access-analyzer/policy-generator tooling (which derives a minimal policy from a principal's actual observed usage) as the starting point for narrowing existing wildcard grants.
Establish a mandatory least-privilege review as part of the IAM-policy-creation process itself, rather than allowing wildcard grants to be created as a default "get it working" starting point.
Periodically re-run access-analyzer reviews across the account to catch policy drift and newly-introduced wildcard grants before they accumulate.
items.mitigationClientFacing: One of your cloud access policies grants far broader permissions than the role using it needs — in effect, wildcards that permit almost any action on almost any resource, which amounts to administrative access regardless of the role's modest name. Over-broad permissions are the raw material of most cloud breaches, because any compromise of that role inherits all of it. The fix is to reduce each policy to the specific actions and resources genuinely required. Watch for permissions assembled across several narrow policies that combine into a broad effect, since reviewing any one of them in isolation misses the total.

items.title: Instance Metadata Service Credential Theft via SSRF (IMDSv1)
items.prerequisites: A cloud-hosted application with a confirmed or suspected server-side request forgery vector — any feature that fetches a URL you supply (webhook validation, link preview, remote image import, PDF rendering, document conversion). Knowledge of the target cloud provider, since each uses a different metadata address and response format. Written authorisation covering credential retrieval, because a successful test yields live production credentials.
items.whatItIs: Every major cloud platform runs a metadata service reachable only from inside an instance, at a fixed link-local address. It answers unauthenticated HTTP requests from that instance and — critically — hands out temporary credentials for the role attached to it. If the application can be made to fetch a URL on the attacker's behalf, the request originates from inside the instance, so the metadata service answers it. The SSRF stops being a curiosity about internal reachability and becomes direct theft of production cloud credentials.
items.rootCause: The metadata service authenticates by network position alone: anything able to send it an HTTP request from the instance is treated as the instance itself. That assumption held when only instance software could reach it, but an SSRF vulnerability turns any external user into an indirect sender. The original protocol (IMDSv1) requires nothing but a plain GET, which is exactly the shape of request a naive URL-fetching feature will happily make. The newer session-oriented protocol (IMDSv2) breaks this by requiring a PUT with a header first, which simple SSRF cannot produce.
items.impact: The attacker obtains the instance role's temporary credentials and can then act as that role directly against the cloud provider's API, from anywhere, with no further access to the application. Because instance roles are frequently over-scoped, this commonly grants read access to storage buckets, databases and secrets stores well beyond what the compromised application itself needed. The activity is also attributed to a legitimate role in audit logs, so it blends into normal service traffic, and the credentials remain valid until they expire on their own schedule.
stepsToIdentify: Establish whether the application is cloud-hosted and on which provider, since the metadata address and required request shape differ between them.

Identify every feature that fetches a caller-supplied URL — webhook targets, link previews, avatar import, PDF or screenshot rendering, XML/document parsers — and confirm the request originates server-side rather than in the browser.
Test whether the fetch reaches internal addresses at all by pointing it at a harmless internal or loopback address and observing the response, error text, or timing difference.
Request the metadata root path and check whether a metadata-shaped response comes back, which confirms IMDSv1 is answering plain GET requests.
If plain requests are refused, determine whether IMDSv2 is enforced (a session token is required first) or whether a network control is blocking the address, since these are very different findings.
Check whether the fetch follows redirects and how it resolves hostnames, since redirect-based and DNS-based approaches defeat naive address blocklists.
exploitationSteps: Confirm in writing that credential retrieval is authorised before proceeding, since the next step returns live production credentials rather than a proof-of-concept value.
Retrieve the role name from the metadata credentials path, and stop there first — the role name alone proves the finding without holding any secret material.
Where full proof is explicitly authorised, retrieve the credential document and verify it is valid with a single, read-only identity call that returns only who the credentials belong to.
Enumerate the role's effective permissions using read-only policy-inspection calls rather than probing by attempting real actions, so the blast radius is documented without exercising it.
Do not use the credentials to access customer data; describe what the permissions would allow instead, and record the specific over-scoped permissions as the remediation target.

Treat any retrieved credential as sensitive engagement material: store it only as long as the finding requires, note the expiry time, and ask the client to revoke the role session at the end of testing.

examplePayloads.label: AWS — list roles exposed to the instance (IMDSv1)
AWS — confirm IMDSv2 is enforced (should fail without a token)
Azure — instance metadata (requires a header, so tests header injection too)
GCP — service account token (requires Metadata-Flavor header)
Bypass probe — alternate encoding of the link-local address
Verify retrieved credentials without touching data

variants: Redirect-based reach where the supplied URL points to an attacker-controlled host that responds with a 302 to the metadata address, defeating a blocklist applied only to the original URL.
DNS rebinding where a hostname resolves to a permitted address during validation and to the metadata address at fetch time.
Container platform variants where the metadata service is reachable from a pod and grants node-level rather than pod-level credentials.
Blind exploitation where the response is never displayed, and the credential is exfiltrated by having the fetch send it to an attacker-controlled endpoint instead.
mitigation: Enforce IMDSv2 (session-token required) instance-wide and disable IMDSv1 entirely, which defeats simple SSRF because the required PUT and header cannot be produced by a naive URL fetch.
Set the metadata hop limit to 1 so containers and nested workloads cannot reach the host's metadata endpoint.
Apply a strict destination allowlist to every server-side fetch, validating after DNS resolution and after each redirect rather than only on the submitted string.
Scope instance roles to the minimum the workload actually needs, so a stolen credential grants little — this is the control that limits impact when the others fail.
Block outbound access to the link-local metadata range from application containers at the network layer where the workload has no legitimate need for it.
Alert on instance-role credentials being used from an IP address outside the cloud provider's own ranges, which is a high-signal indicator this has already happened.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A server-side request weakness in one of your applications can be pointed at the cloud platform's internal information service, which hands back the temporary credentials the server itself uses. This is why such a weakness is routinely critical in a cloud environment rather than moderate: it converts a request-forgery bug into working cloud credentials and a foothold in your account. The fix has two parts — repair the application weakness, and enforce the platform's newer, hardened version of that internal service, which defeats the naive form of this attack. Both matter: the hardened service is a strong safety net, but the application flaw should still be fixed.

tools: Cloud provider CLI for read-only identity verification
SSRF payload lists for encoding and redirect variants

items.title: IAM Privilege Escalation via Permission Chaining
items.prerequisites: Valid credentials for a low-privileged cloud principal — a developer user, a CI/CD service account, or a role obtained from another finding. Read access to policy documents (or the ability to infer permissions by attempting read-only calls). Written authorisation covering privilege escalation testing, since a successful chain results in genuinely elevated access in a live account.
items.whatItIs: This is distinct from a single over-permissive policy: each individual permission looks reasonable in isolation, but combining them produces an escalation path the reviewer never intended. Permission to create a new version of a policy, to attach a policy to yourself, to pass a role to a service, or to update a function's execution role are all defensible grants on their own — and each is also a route from low privilege to administrator. The vulnerability is the composition, which is why policy reviews that examine grants one at a time consistently miss it.
items.rootCause: Cloud IAM evaluates each permission independently and has no concept of 'this combination is equivalent to administrator'. Policies also accumulate: a permission granted for a one-off task is rarely revoked, and permissions attached to shared roles grow over time as new use cases appear. Because writing a tightly-scoped policy requires knowing the exact action list in advance, teams grant broader service-level permissions and rely on the assumption that nobody will chain them — an assumption nothing in the platform enforces.
items.impact: A compromised low-privilege credential — a leaked developer key, an over-trusted CI token, an SSRF-obtained instance role — becomes full administrative control of the cloud account. From there the attacker can read every data store, disable logging, create persistent backdoor principals, and remove the evidence of how they arrived. Because each step uses a permission the principal legitimately holds, none of the individual API calls looks anomalous, and detection depends on recognising the sequence rather than any single event.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the current principal's effective permissions using read-only policy-inspection calls, including policies inherited through group and role membership rather than only those attached directly.

Identify permissions in the known escalation categories: creating or modifying policy versions, attaching policies, passing roles to services, creating access keys for other principals, and updating the execution role of compute resources.
For each candidate, determine what it can actually reach — a role-passing permission is only dangerous in combination with permission to create or update something that will assume that role.
Map which higher-privileged roles the principal could reach, and confirm whether their trust policies would actually permit the assumption.
Run an automated IAM path-analysis tool where scope allows, then verify its findings manually, since these tools report theoretical paths that trust policies or conditions may block in practice.
Check whether service control policies or permission boundaries are in place, since they can neutralise an otherwise-valid escalation path and change the finding's severity substantially.
exploitationSteps: Confirm in writing that escalation is authorised and agree what the end state should be, since demonstrating a path means genuinely holding elevated permissions in a live account.
Demonstrate the shortest confirmed chain rather than the most elaborate, since the shortest path is the one remediation must break.
Prefer creating a clearly-labelled temporary artefact — a distinctly named policy version or role — over modifying anything the client already relies on, so cleanup is unambiguous.
Verify elevation with a read-only call that only proves the new permission level, rather than exercising it against real resources.
Record every artefact created with its exact identifier and timestamp, and remove them at the end of testing, then confirm removal with the client.
Report the specific permission combination that made the chain possible, not merely 'IAM is over-permissive' — the fix is removing one link, and the client needs to know which.

variants: Compute-based escalation where the principal cannot assume a role directly but can attach it to a function or instance it controls, then read the credentials from inside.
Policy-version escalation where the principal can create a new version of an existing policy and set it as default, rewriting its own permissions.
Trust-policy modification where the principal can edit a privileged role's trust document to add itself as an allowed assumer.
Escalation through a CI/CD pipeline, where the ability to modify a build definition grants the pipeline's much broader role.
mitigation: Apply permission boundaries to every non-administrative principal, capping the maximum privilege reachable regardless of which policies get attached later.
Treat the escalation-enabling actions as privileged: restrict policy modification, role passing, and execution-role updates to a small, separately-governed set of principals.
Constrain role-passing permissions with an explicit condition naming which roles may be passed and to which service, rather than granting the action broadly.
Run automated IAM path analysis continuously in CI rather than at audit time, so a newly-introduced escalation path is caught when the policy changes.
Review permissions in combination rather than individually, since every finding in this class is composed of grants that each looked acceptable alone.
Alert on the escalation-enabling API calls themselves — policy version creation, trust policy edits, role attachment — which are rare in normal operation and therefore high-signal.
items.mitigationClientFacing: An attacker who gains a low-privilege foothold in your cloud account can climb to full administrative control by chaining together individually-minor permissions, each of which grants the ability to acquire the next. No single permission looks dangerous; the danger is in the sequence. This is one of the most important findings in a cloud review because it defeats the assumption that a limited account stays limited. The fix is to identify and break these escalation chains — typically by removing permissions that let a principal grant itself further access — and to review access as a whole rather than one policy at a time, since the chain is only visible in aggregate.

items.title: Public Exposure via Resource-Based Policies on Queues, Topics and Functions
items.prerequisites: Read access to the cloud account's resource configuration, or the ability to test access anonymously from outside it. An understanding of which resource types in the environment support resource-based policies, which typically includes queues, notification topics, functions, key vaults, container registries and log destinations. Authorisation to attempt anonymous access from outside the account.
items.whatItIs: Public storage buckets are well known and usually checked. The same policy mechanism applies to a long list of other resource types where it is almost never reviewed. A queue whose policy grants send permission to any principal can be written to by anyone on the internet, and a topic with open subscribe permission can be read by anyone. These resources carry the messages that drive processing, so access to them often means influence over the systems that consume them.
items.rootCause: Resource-based policies are edited directly rather than through a managed interface, and the wildcard principal is a quick way to make an integration work during development. Public-access blocks are usually implemented for storage only, so the same guardrail does not exist for other services. Console warnings about public exposure are prominent for buckets and largely absent elsewhere, so the configuration looks unremarkable in review.
items.impact: An open queue or topic lets an attacker inject messages that downstream consumers process as trusted input, which frequently reaches internal systems with no further authentication. An open subscription discloses whatever flows through the topic, which is often transaction or event data. A publicly invocable function executes with its own role's permissions, so anyone on the internet can act with that role. None of these show up in a storage-focused public exposure review.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every resource type in the account that supports a resource-based policy, rather than checking storage alone.
Retrieve each policy and identify statements granting access to a wildcard principal or to an entire organisation.
Check whether any condition keys constrain a broad principal, since an unconstrained wildcard is the dangerous case.
Determine whether account-level public access blocks exist for these services, or only for storage.
Test anonymous access from outside the account for anything that appears open, since policy evaluation may still deny it.
Identify what consumes each queue or topic, because the downstream consumer determines the real impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope permits anonymous access attempts against the account's resources from outside it.
Enumerate policies across all supported resource types and shortlist those with a wildcard principal.
From an unauthenticated context, attempt the least intrusive permitted operation — a metadata read or an attribute query.
For a writable queue, send a single benign marker message rather than anything a consumer would act on.
Trace whether the marker reached a consumer, which is what distinguishes an exposed resource from an exploitable path.
For a publicly invocable function, confirm invocation is possible and stop before exercising its role's permissions.

examplePayloads.command: aws sqs list-queues --query 'QueueUrls[]' --output text | xargs -I{} aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url {} --attribute-names Policy

examplePayloads.label: Find wildcard principals
examplePayloads.command: # extract each policy and flag statements where Effect is Allow and Principal is "*" with no Condition

examplePayloads.label: Topic policy review
examplePayloads.command: aws sns list-topics --query 'Topics[].TopicArn' --output text | xargs -I{} aws sns get-topic-attributes --topic-arn {}

Benign marker message
Function policy check

variants: A key vault or secrets store whose access policy grants a broad principal, exposing credentials directly.
A container registry open for anonymous pull, disclosing application images and any secrets baked into them.
A log destination writable by any principal, allowing an attacker to inject or flood audit records.
A policy scoped to an entire organisation rather than a wildcard, which is narrower but still far broader than intended.
mitigation: Apply policy-as-code checks that reject any resource policy with a wildcard principal and no constraining condition, across all resource types.
Enable account-level public access blocks for every service that offers them, not only for storage.
Require a condition on any broad principal grant, such as a source account, organisation identifier or network restriction.
Scan the estate continuously for newly public resources rather than relying on review at creation time.
Authenticate and authorise message consumers on message content, so an injected message is not automatically trusted.
Include non-storage resource types in the public exposure review, since that is the gap this finding lives in.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Some of your cloud resources — message queues, notification channels and similar — carry their own access policies, and several of those are set to permit public or broad access, exposing the data flowing through them. These resource-attached policies are easy to overlook because they sit on individual services rather than in the central access configuration. The fix is to review the policy on each such resource and restrict it to the specific principals that need it. This is a sweep-and-tighten exercise across your services, and it matters because these channels frequently carry sensitive operational data that is assumed to be internal.

tools: Policy-as-code tooling such as OPA or Checkov

items.title: Backup and Snapshot Ransomware Resilience Failure
items.prerequisites: Read access to the account's backup, snapshot and lifecycle configuration, and to the identity policies that govern them. Agreement on whether deletion may be attempted against a designated test resource, since demonstrating the weakness requires attempting destruction. A restore test requires coordination with the operations team.
items.whatItIs: The question is not whether backups exist but whether they survive an attacker with the same permissions as the operations team. In most accounts the identity that creates backups can also delete them, so a single compromised operator credential removes both the production data and the means of recovery. Backups frequently sit in the same account and region as what they protect, which means one account compromise covers everything.
items.rootCause: Backup permissions are granted together because the same team performs create, restore and cleanup, and separating them adds operational friction. Lifecycle rules that delete old snapshots need delete permission by design, and that permission is often attached broadly. Immutability features exist on most platforms but are off by default and require deliberate configuration. Cross-account backup copies are extra work with no visible benefit until the day they are needed.
items.impact: Ransomware against a cloud estate targets backups first precisely because this configuration is common. Where backups can be deleted by the same credential that reaches production, the organisation's recovery position is no better than its prevention. The consequence is total: encrypted or deleted production data with no restore path, which converts a contained incident into an existential one. Untested restores produce the same outcome more slowly.
stepsToIdentify: Inventory what is backed up and confirm whether coverage matches the systems the organisation considers critical.
Determine where backups are stored: the same account and region, a different region, or a separate account entirely.
Identify which identities can delete backups, snapshots or the vault holding them.
Check whether immutability or object lock is enabled, and whether the retention period matches the recovery objective.
Establish whether deletion requires multi-factor authentication or a second approval.
Review when a restore was last tested end to end, and whether the test measured time to recover.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, and agree that deletion attempts target only a designated test resource.
Using an operator-level credential, enumerate the snapshots and backup vaults reachable with it.
Attempt deletion of a designated test snapshot and record whether it succeeds, is denied, or is blocked by a lock.
Where deletion is blocked, identify which control blocked it, since that distinguishes immutability from a policy denial.
Attempt to modify the retention or lifecycle policy, since weakening retention achieves the same end more quietly.
Report the finding as the smallest set of permissions that would remove the recovery path, which is what makes it actionable.

Vault access policy
Immutability check
Who can delete
examplePayloads.command: # enumerate identities whose effective permissions include snapshot and vault delete actions

examplePayloads.label: Controlled deletion attempt
Retention weakening attempt

variants: Backups in the same account as production, so one account compromise covers both.
Lifecycle rules that can be edited to expire backups immediately, achieving deletion without a delete call.
Encryption keys for backups deletable by the same identity, which renders backups unusable without touching them.
Replicas treated as backups, where deletion or encryption propagates to the replica automatically.
mitigation: Store backups in a separate account with a trust relationship that permits write and restore but not delete from the production account.
Enable immutability or object lock with a retention period at least as long as the recovery objective.
Separate backup creation from backup deletion permissions, and require a second approval for deletion.
Protect encryption keys used for backups with the same separation, since losing the key is equivalent to losing the backup.
Alert on snapshot deletion, retention policy changes and vault policy changes, treating them as potential incident indicators.
Test a full restore on a schedule and record the time taken, since an untested backup is an assumption rather than a control.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your backups and snapshots are not protected against an attacker who reaches them, which is the specific weakness that turns a ransomware incident from recoverable into catastrophic — modern ransomware deliberately destroys backups first, precisely so you cannot restore. The fix is to make backups resilient to this: keep copies that cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, hold at least one copy isolated from the account that could be compromised, and test that a restore actually works. This is a resilience control rather than a preventive one, and it is the difference between an expensive disruption and an existential one.

items.title: Overly Permissive Kubernetes RBAC and Cluster-Admin Binding
items.prerequisites: Read access to a Kubernetes cluster's role and binding configuration, or credentials for a service account whose effective permissions are being assessed. Cluster access through kubectl with at least read permission on RBAC resources. Authorisation to enumerate permissions and, where agreed, to demonstrate escalation using a designated test namespace.
items.whatItIs: Kubernetes RBAC is precise but verbose, and the shortest path to making something work is a broad binding. The result is clusters where service accounts hold permissions far beyond what their workload needs. Several individually reasonable-looking permissions are also escalation paths in themselves: the ability to create pods, to read secrets, to modify role bindings, or to create tokens for other service accounts each lead to cluster-admin by a short route.
items.rootCause: Default roles are coarse, and binding the built-in cluster-admin role resolves a permissions problem immediately while a precise role takes iteration. Bindings to broad subjects such as all authenticated users or all service accounts are sometimes applied during troubleshooting and left in place. The escalation potential of specific verbs is not obvious from the manifest, so a review that checks for cluster-admin by name will miss a role that reaches it indirectly.
items.impact: Cluster-admin is complete control of every workload, secret and node in the cluster. Reaching it from a compromised application pod turns a single application vulnerability into control of everything the cluster runs, including other tenants where the cluster is shared. Because the cloud node identity is usually reachable from a privileged pod, the escalation frequently continues out of the cluster into the cloud account itself.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all cluster role bindings and identify every subject bound to cluster-admin.
Look for bindings to broad subjects such as all authenticated users, all service accounts, or an entire namespace's default account.
Enumerate roles granting wildcard verbs or wildcard resources, which are equivalent to cluster-admin within their scope.
Identify escalation-capable verbs specifically: creating pods, reading secrets, creating service account tokens, and modifying bindings.
Determine which service accounts are actually mounted into running pods, since an unused permissive account is a lower priority.
Check whether the default service account is automounted, which grants its permissions to every pod that does not opt out.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers permission enumeration and agree whether demonstration is permitted in a designated test namespace.
From a workload's service account context, enumerate effective permissions rather than reading manifests alone.
Identify the shortest escalation path available from that context and document each step in the chain.
Where demonstration is authorised, execute the chain in the test namespace and stop at the first proof of elevated capability.
Confirm whether the path reaches the node identity, which would extend the compromise into the cloud account.
Report the path as a sequence, since each individual permission may look defensible while the chain is not.

examplePayloads.label: Find cluster-admin bindings
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .metadata.name + " -> " + (.subjects // [] | map(.kind+"/"+.name) | join(","))'

examplePayloads.label: Broad subject bindings
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select((.subjects // [])[]?.name | test("system:authenticated|system:serviceaccounts")) | .metadata.name'

examplePayloads.label: Wildcard roles
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select((.rules // [])[]? | (.verbs[]?=="*") and (.resources[]?=="*")) | .metadata.name'

examplePayloads.label: Effective permissions from a context
Escalation-capable verbs
examplePayloads.command: kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> && kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>

examplePayloads.label: Automount check

variants: Secret read permission alone, which yields whatever credentials other workloads hold without any binding change.
Pod creation permission, allowing a pod to be scheduled with a more privileged service account attached.
Permission to create service account tokens, granting the identity of any account in scope.
Aggregated cluster roles where a label change silently widens an existing role's permissions.
mitigation: Bind cluster-admin only to named human administrators, never to service accounts or to broad subjects.
Grant workloads a role scoped to the specific resources and verbs they need, and derive that from observed usage rather than guesswork.
Disable automounting of the default service account token, requiring workloads to opt in explicitly.
Treat secret read, pod create, token create and binding modify as privileged, and review every grant of them individually.
Run automated RBAC analysis in the pipeline to detect escalation paths before they are deployed.
Restrict the node identity's cloud permissions so that cluster compromise does not automatically extend into the account.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Access within your container platform is granted too broadly, with more identities holding cluster-wide administrative rights than the environment needs. Anyone — or anything — holding that level of access controls the entire cluster and everything running on it, so each unnecessary grant is an oversized target. The fix is to reduce these permissions to the minimum each user and workload genuinely requires, and in particular to remove cluster-wide administrative rights from anything that does not truly need them. This is a least-privilege exercise, and in a container platform it is especially important because the blast radius of a compromised administrative identity is the whole cluster.

items.title: Insecure Kubernetes Secret Storage and Distribution
items.prerequisites: Access to a Kubernetes cluster with permission to read secrets in at least one namespace, or a workload context from which secret access can be assessed. Visibility of the cluster's encryption-at-rest configuration, which for managed clusters may require provider console access. Authorisation to enumerate secrets without recording their values.
items.whatItIs: A Kubernetes secret is base64-encoded, not encrypted, and the encoding is frequently mistaken for protection. Whether the stored value is actually encrypted depends on an encryption-at-rest provider being configured for etcd, which is not the default on self-managed clusters. Secrets are also commonly mounted into pods that do not need them, or injected as environment variables where they appear in process listings, crash dumps and logs.
items.rootCause: The name suggests protection that the default configuration does not provide. Environment variable injection is the most convenient distribution method and is what most documentation demonstrates, despite environment variables being readable from the process table and captured in diagnostics. Secrets tend to be created once and never rotated because rotation requires a coordinated workload restart, so a long-lived secret accumulates exposure.
items.impact: Anyone who can read secrets in a namespace holds the credentials for everything those workloads reach: databases, cloud accounts, third-party services. Where etcd is unencrypted, anyone with access to an etcd backup has the same. Environment-injected secrets leak into logs and crash reports routinely, which spreads them to systems never intended to hold credentials. Because secrets are rarely rotated, exposure persists long after the access that caused it.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether encryption at rest is configured for secrets, and which provider is in use.
Enumerate which identities and service accounts can read secrets, and in which namespaces.
Identify how secrets reach workloads: mounted volumes, environment variables, or an external secrets operator.
Check whether any secret is mounted into pods that do not require it, particularly through broad volume definitions.
Review whether application logs or crash handlers could capture environment variables.
Establish whether secrets are rotated, and how long the oldest in use has existed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers secret enumeration and agree that values will not be recorded in the report.
From a workload context, test whether secrets are readable and in which namespaces.
Enumerate secret names and types without decoding values, to establish scope of exposure.
Where a secret is proven readable, verify its type and the resource it protects rather than using the credential.
Inspect a running pod's environment to confirm whether secrets are exposed in the process environment.
Report per credential type and per blast radius, since the impact is determined by what each secret unlocks.

examplePayloads.label: Encryption-at-rest configuration
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get apiserver -o yaml 2>/dev/null | grep -A5 encryption   # or inspect the provider's cluster configuration

examplePayloads.label: Who can read secrets
Enumerate without decoding
Environment exposure check
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select((.spec.containers[].env // [])[]?.valueFrom.secretKeyRef) | .metadata.name'

examplePayloads.label: In-pod environment
Secret age
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.creationTimestamp + " " + .metadata.name' | sort

variants: Secrets committed to a Git repository as manifests, exposing them to everyone with repository access.
An unencrypted etcd backup stored where it is more broadly accessible than the cluster itself.
Secrets passed as container image build arguments, persisting in image layers.
An external secrets operator with an over-broad cloud role, so compromising it yields the entire secret store.
mitigation: Enable encryption at rest for secrets with a provider backed by a managed key service rather than a local key.
Mount secrets as files rather than injecting them as environment variables, so they do not appear in the process environment or in diagnostics.
Restrict secret read permission per namespace and per service account, and review every grant.
Use an external secret store with short-lived dynamically issued credentials in preference to long-lived static secrets.
Rotate secrets on a schedule and build the workload restart into that process so rotation is operationally routine.
Protect etcd backups to the same standard as the cluster, since an unencrypted backup discloses every secret.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The secrets your container platform uses — passwords, keys, tokens — are stored and distributed insecurely, so an attacker who reaches the cluster, or an over-privileged workload within it, can read them. Because these secrets typically unlock other systems, exposure here spreads outward. The fix is to store them encrypted, to restrict which workloads and users can read each one, and ideally to source them from a dedicated secret store rather than holding them in the cluster's own basic storage. This pairs with the access-control finding: tightening who can read secrets is only effective if the secrets are also protected at rest.

items.title: Audit Logging Gaps and Mutable Trail Configuration
items.prerequisites: Read access to the account's logging configuration, including trail definitions, log destinations and their access policies. Visibility of retention settings and of which identities can modify logging configuration. Authorisation to attempt a configuration change against a designated non-production trail where a demonstration is agreed.
items.whatItIs: This is distinct from logs being exposed: here the concern is whether the record exists at all and whether it survives an attacker. Common gaps are a trail covering only one region while activity occurs in others, data-plane events not recorded so object access is invisible, logs written to a bucket in the same account with no immutability, and the same identities that can act being able to edit or delete the record of having acted.
items.rootCause: Logging is enabled once at account creation and rarely revisited as the estate grows into new regions and services. Data-plane logging is off by default because it is voluminous and billed by volume, so the events most useful for investigating a data breach are the ones most often missing. The log destination is placed in the same account for convenience, which means an identity with sufficient permissions can reach both the activity and its record.
items.impact: Without a complete, tamper-resistant trail the organisation cannot determine what an attacker did, which prevents scoping an incident and therefore prevents accurate notification. An attacker who can disable or delete logging removes the evidence of everything that follows, and the gap itself is often not alerted on. Where regulation requires demonstrable audit records, the deficiency is a compliance finding independent of any incident.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether a trail exists, whether it is multi-region, and whether it covers all accounts in the organisation.
Determine whether data-plane events are recorded for storage and other data services, not only management events.
Identify the log destination and whether it sits in a separate account from the workloads it records.
Check whether log integrity validation and object immutability are enabled on the destination.
Enumerate which identities can stop, delete or reconfigure the trail, and whether any alert exists for those actions.
Compare retention against the organisation's stated investigation window and any regulatory requirement.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, and agree that configuration changes target only a designated non-production trail.
Enumerate trails and record coverage gaps by region, account and event type.
Using an operator-level credential, enumerate which logging actions that identity is permitted to perform.
On the designated test trail, attempt to stop logging and record whether it succeeds and whether anything alerts.
Attempt to modify the log destination policy or lifecycle rule, since either can remove records without a delete call.
Restore the original configuration and report the smallest permission set that would create a blind spot.

Data-plane event check
Log integrity validation

variants: A trail configured in one region while workloads run in several, so activity elsewhere is unrecorded.
Logs delivered to a bucket with a lifecycle rule expiring them well before the investigation window.
Kubernetes audit logging disabled on a managed cluster, leaving cluster activity invisible even where cloud logging is complete.
Organisation member accounts excluded from the organisation trail, creating per-account blind spots.
mitigation: Enable a multi-region organisation trail covering every account, and verify coverage rather than assuming inheritance.
Record data-plane events for services holding sensitive data, accepting the volume cost for the systems that warrant it.
Deliver logs to a dedicated logging account that workload identities cannot write to or delete from.
Enable log file integrity validation and object immutability with retention matching the investigation window.
Alert on any change to logging configuration, treating a stop or delete as an incident until proven otherwise.
Verify periodically that logs are actually arriving, since a silently broken delivery looks identical to a quiet estate.
items.mitigationClientFacing: There are gaps in your cloud audit logging, and in places the log trail can be altered or switched off, which means some activity in your account is either unrecorded or could be erased by an attacker covering their tracks. Without a complete, tamper-resistant record, you cannot reliably investigate an incident or demonstrate what did and did not happen — which is often a regulatory requirement in its own right. The fix is to ensure logging covers all activity, is enabled across every region, and is written somewhere it cannot be modified or deleted, including by an administrator. This underpins your ability to respond to every other finding here.

items.title: Container Registry Exposure and Unsigned Image Deployment
items.prerequisites: Knowledge of the container registries the environment pulls from, whether managed, self-hosted or public. Read access to registry configuration and to the cluster or service admission configuration. Authorisation to attempt anonymous pull against registries in scope, and to push a test image to a designated repository where a demonstration is agreed.
items.whatItIs: Two related weaknesses sit at the registry boundary. The first is exposure: registries configured for anonymous pull disclose application images, which commonly contain embedded configuration, credentials and internal source. The second is trust: most clusters pull by mutable tag with no signature verification, so whatever currently sits at that tag is what runs. Anyone who can push to the repository can therefore change what production executes.
items.rootCause: Anonymous pull is enabled to simplify deployment and then forgotten, and self-hosted registries frequently ship with it on by default. Tag-based deployment is the documented norm despite tags being mutable pointers rather than content identifiers. Signature verification requires an admission controller and a key management process, which is additional work with no immediate functional benefit, so it is deferred and rarely revisited.
items.impact: An exposed registry hands an attacker the application's internals and any secrets baked into its layers, which is frequently enough on its own. The absence of signature verification means a compromised build pipeline, a stolen push credential or a typosquatted base image results in attacker-controlled code running in production with the workload's full identity. Because the image name looks correct, neither deployment logs nor a manifest review reveals anything unusual.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every registry the environment pulls from, including public base images referenced in Dockerfiles.
Test anonymous pull against each registry and repository in scope.
Determine whether deployments reference mutable tags or immutable content digests.
Check whether an admission controller enforces signature verification, and whether it fails closed.
Identify who holds push credentials to production repositories, including pipeline identities.
Inspect image layers for embedded secrets, which is both a finding in itself and what makes registry exposure serious.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers anonymous pull attempts and, where agreed, a push to a designated test repository.
Attempt an unauthenticated catalog listing and tag listing against each registry.
Pull an image anonymously where permitted and inspect its layers and configuration for embedded credentials.
Check whether any recovered credential is still valid, by structure rather than by authenticating, unless separately authorised.
Where push is authorised, push a benign marker image to a designated test tag and confirm whether it deploys unchallenged.
Report whether signature verification blocked the deployment, since that single control determines the severity.

Anonymous tag listing
Anonymous pull
Layer secret inspection

examplePayloads.label: Tag versus digest check
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' | grep -v '@sha256:' | sort -u

examplePayloads.command: # deploy an unsigned benign marker image to a test namespace and record whether admission rejects it

variants: A public registry mirror inside the environment that caches images without verifying their origin.
Dependency confusion at the image level, where a public repository shadows an intended internal name.
A compromised base image in a build pipeline, inherited by every derived image without review.
Tag mutation on an otherwise legitimate image, changing what runs without any manifest change.
mitigation: Disable anonymous pull on all registries and require authentication even for internal networks.
Deploy by immutable digest rather than by tag, so what was tested is what runs.
Sign images at build time and enforce verification with an admission controller configured to fail closed.
Restrict push permission on production repositories to the build pipeline identity alone, and protect that identity accordingly.
Scan images for embedded secrets in the pipeline and fail the build, since registry exposure is only serious because of what images contain.
Mirror approved base images into a controlled registry and build only from that mirror.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your container image registry is exposed more broadly than it should be, and images can be deployed without verifying they are genuine and unmodified. Together these let an attacker read your images — including any secrets in them — and potentially get a tampered image deployed into your environment. The fix is to restrict access to the registry and to require that every image is cryptographically signed and its signature checked before it runs, so an unsigned or altered image is refused. This closes a supply-chain path into your running environment, where a substituted image executes with the access of the workload it replaces.

items.title: Workforce Identity Federation Trust Misconfiguration
items.prerequisites: Read access to the cloud account's identity provider configuration and to the roles that federated users assume. Understanding of which external identity provider issues assertions and which attributes drive role assignment. Authorisation to review trust policies and, where agreed, to test assertion handling against a designated non-production role.
items.whatItIs: Federation makes the external identity provider the authority over who gets cloud access, and the trust configuration decides how far that authority reaches. The failures are in the conditions rather than in the protocol: a role whose trust policy accepts any identity from the provider rather than a specific group, attribute mapping driven by a claim the user can influence, or a provider left configured after a migration and still trusted. Any of these means an account in the external directory becomes an account in the cloud.
items.rootCause: Trust policies are written once during the federation project and scoped broadly to get every team working, with the intention of tightening later. Attribute-based role assignment depends on claims whose provenance is not always verified, and group membership in a large directory is frequently self-service or delegated. Decommissioned providers are rarely removed because nothing breaks when they remain, and audience and issuer conditions are optional fields that are easy to omit.
items.impact: An attacker who obtains any account in the external directory, or who can influence the attributes on one, obtains cloud access with whatever the mapped role permits. This bypasses the cloud provider's own controls entirely because the authentication is legitimate and the assertion is valid. Where a role is broadly scoped, a single low-value directory account becomes broad account access. Detection is difficult because the sign-in looks exactly like a normal federated login.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every configured identity provider, including any left from a migration or a decommissioned partner.
Review each role's trust policy and determine whether it accepts any identity from the provider or requires a specific group or attribute.
Identify which claims drive role assignment and establish who can modify those attributes in the source directory.
Check whether audience and issuer conditions are present, since omitting them widens the trust considerably.
Determine whether session duration and permission boundaries constrain what a federated session can do.
Assess whether directory group membership is self-service, which would let a user grant themselves a mapped role.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers federation testing and agree that any demonstration targets a designated non-production role.
Map the full path from directory account to cloud permissions, recording every condition evaluated along the way.
Identify the weakest link: a missing condition, a user-modifiable attribute, or a self-service group.
Where authorised, use a low-privilege directory account to assume the designated role and confirm the path works end to end.
Record what the assumed session could reach, by enumerating permissions rather than exercising them.
Report the specific condition whose absence permits the path, since that is the single change that closes it.

variants: An OIDC provider trusted without a subject condition, so any workload from that provider can assume the role.
A stale provider left configured after a migration, where the tester or an attacker may still control an account.
Attribute mapping driven by a user-editable profile field such as department or title.
A self-service directory group mapped to a privileged role, allowing a user to grant themselves access.
mitigation: Condition every trust policy on a specific group or attribute, never accepting any identity from the provider.
Require audience and issuer conditions on every federated trust relationship.
Map roles from attributes the user cannot modify, and restrict membership changes on any group that grants cloud access.
Remove identity providers as part of decommissioning, and audit the provider list on a schedule.
Apply permission boundaries and short session durations to federated roles so a misconfiguration has a bounded effect.
Alert on federated assumption of privileged roles, particularly from unusual source networks or outside working hours.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The trust relationship that lets your workforce identity system sign people in to the cloud is misconfigured, in a way that could let someone authenticate as a user they are not, or gain access they were not granted. Because this sits at the front door of your cloud environment, a weakness here can undermine the access controls behind it. The fix is to correct the federation trust so it accepts only the intended identity provider and maps identities and their permissions exactly as intended. This warrants prompt attention, as identity federation is the foundation the rest of your cloud access control is built on.
